item.title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
item.dc:creator: Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad

Topics: Persuasion, Social identity, Narrative persuasion, Social influence

Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

item.title: How Chinese and U.S. media construct legitimacy at sea differently: A corpus-based comparative analysis of China’s distant-water fishing
item.dc:creator: Cheng Chen, Renping Liu
item.description:
Journalism · Cheng Chen, Renping Liu

Topics: Media framing, Journalism, Comparative media systems, Sentiment analysis

Journalism plays a vital role in shaping how societies interpret and legitimize global environmental controversies. This study compares how Chinese and U.S. media discursively frame China’s distant-water fishing (DWF)—a domain where environmental, economic, and geopolitical interests intersect. Using a corpus-based mixed-method approach that integrates sentiment analysis, keyword extraction, and nomination strategies, the research analyzes 167 English-language news articles from leading outlets in both countries to uncover how legitimacy is communicatively constructed within distinct media systems. The findings reveal two coherent yet contrasting framing logics. U.S. media adopt a critical and moralized framing that emphasizes illegality, environmental harm, and systemic accountability, reflecting a liberal-institutionalist orientation rooted in watchdog journalism and rule-based governance. Chinese media, in contrast, employ a more procedural and developmental framing that highlights regulation, cooperation, and economic pragmatism, reflecting a greater emphasis on institutional coordination, policy implementation, and national development priorities. The study advances comparative journalism research by linking media framing with policy paradigms, showing how institutional and communicative contexts shape the realization of ostensibly universal news values such as Negativity and Eliteness. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of combining computational and qualitative discourse analysis to reveal patterned differences in journalistic representation. Substantively, it underscores journalism’s dual role in global environmental discourse—as both a site where legitimacy and responsibility are contested, and a communicative bridge that may either intensify conflict or foster mutual understanding in governing shared environmental commons.

item.title: The managed sisterhood: Gendered labor and intimacy in Chinese fashion influencer industry
item.dc:creator: Qiheng Lin, Chenyu Dong
item.description:
New Media & Society · Qiheng Lin, Chenyu Dong

Topics: Gender differences, Platform studies, Social media influencers, Digital labor

As China’s leading multi-channel network (MCN) institutions become increasingly industrialized and bureaucratic, their operations are paradoxically characterized by intensified emotional dynamics. Drawing on ethnographic research within a women-dominated fashion influencer team, this study identifies a sisterhood-based production model that embeds sisterly ties within hierarchical organizational structures. It traces the formation and collapse of this managed sisterhood. By cultivating an illusion of unity and belonging, intimacy makes labor more governable, obscuring coercion while facilitating the mobilization of emotional, aesthetic, and physical capacities. In this way, sisterhood becomes integral to production, intensifying labor and rendering precarity routine. Under platform capitalism, traditional Chinese sisterhood, once grounded in kinship and flexible resistance, is reconfigured into an occupational form of informal labor control, producing “disposable kinship” in which affective bonds become temporary and replaceable. This study challenges dominant political readings of sisterhood and demonstrates how intimacy itself becomes a mechanism of governance within platform capitalism.

item.title: The news production circuit: Tracing the implementation of constructive journalism
item.dc:creator: Jacob Christian Eriksen, Peter Bro
item.description:
Journalism · Jacob Christian Eriksen, Peter Bro

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, News production, Newsroom practices

Constructive journalism is increasingly invoked in newsroom strategies, educational programs, and professional debates. Yet scholarship has struggled to account for how constructive ambitions are implemented in practice over time. Existing research tends to cluster around partially disconnected domains – such as professional discourse, newsroom initiatives, and content and audience effects – without specifying the dynamic, on-going processes that link organizational decisions to editorial action and the resulting news products. This conceptual article addresses that gap by introducing an analytical framework – the MAP model (Mechanics, Actions, Products) – that conceptualizes implementation as recurring production pathways connecting organizational conditions, situated newswork, and published output. Implementation relies on sustaining these pathways through feedback loops that carry evaluations back into subsequent cycles of production. A pathway may be reinforced and repeated or left unsupported and abandoned, depending on whether the output’s value is registered and recognized. Together, these domains and processes constitute the news production circuit. The article demonstrates the analytical value of MAP through three distinct implementation configurations derived from recent research on constructive journalism. In doing so, it provides a vocabulary for comparative research on how journalistic practices, more generally, are implemented – and for identifying where and why implementation remains partial, uneven, or fragile.

item.title: Dependence or Interdependence? A Folk-Theories Perspective on Journalists’ and Activists’ Mutual Perceptions
item.dc:creator: Marlene Strehler-Schaaf, Charlotte Löb
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Marlene Strehler-Schaaf, Charlotte Löb

Topics: Social movements, Journalism, Journalistic roles, Public opinion

Drawing on folk theories , this study explores how mutual perceptions and experiences shape the journalist–activist relationship. We analyze data from two German interview studies: activists from diverse protest movements ( N = 33) and journalists covering them ( N = 38). Both groups tend to hold simplified views of each other’s work yet apply similar criteria when evaluating “good” journalism/activism and affirm the importance of their roles for democracy. Conflicts often arise from unmet expectations. The study offers insights into how journalism is understood in movement contexts and vice versa. It also clarifies the recently debated boundaries between journalism and activism.

item.title: The democratic value of local information: How journalistic and non-journalistic sources relate to community attachment, civic engagement, and democratic attitudes
item.dc:creator: Leyla Dogruel, Jakob Henke, Wiebke Moehring
item.description:
Journalism · Leyla Dogruel, Jakob Henke, Wiebke Moehring

Topics: Local news, Civic engagement, Media use, Political participation

This study investigates the relationship between local information use, community integration, and political attitudes within the German context. Drawing on representative survey data from 2069 citizens, we examine how using journalistic and non-journalistic local information sources, specifically official municipal sources, community-based sources and interpersonal communication, relates to community attachment, civic engagement, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics. Results indicate that, consistent with previous scholarship, frequent local media use is positively associated with stronger community attachment, higher civic engagement, and more favorable evaluations of local politics and local democracy. Compared to non-journalistic sources of information, local media emerged as stronger predictors of community attachment, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics, but not civic engagement. Our findings highlight the need for closer examination of how the growing diversity of local information sources impact community integration and civic engagements in an increasingly hybrid media environment.

item.title: Invisible Women in Economics: Almost Two Centuries of Gender Representation in the Financial Times and The Economist (1843–2021)
item.dc:creator: Andrea Barigazzi
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Andrea Barigazzi

Topics: Gender representation, Journalism studies, Content analysis, News coverage

This study examines gender representation in the Financial Times and The Economist between 1843 and 2021. Using millions of articles and name-frequency analysis, it traces the long-term evolution of women’s visibility in economic news. Results reveal a U -shaped pattern: relatively high representation in the nineteenth century, a decline through much of the 20th century, and a gradual recovery since the 1980s. Comparisons with benchmarks of women’s participation in high-status occupations and economic sectors show a persistent gap between media visibility and real-world presence. The findings point to a lasting paper ceiling in economic journalism. JEL codes: J16, N34, L82

item.title: Digital transformation in Public Service Media: Adaptation strategies of European broadcasters
item.dc:creator: Clara Almeida Santos, Felisbela Lopes
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Clara Almeida Santos, Felisbela Lopes

Topics: Digital transformation, Public service media, Platformization, Digital platforms

Public Service Media (PSM) are currently undergoing a structural transformation driven by the digitalization of the media ecosystem. Audience fragmentation, the emergence of multi-platform environments and the growing centrality of digital platforms are compelling public service broadcasters to rethink their organizational models, editorial practices and content distribution strategies. This article examines how different European PSM organizations are responding to these challenges and explores how digital transition processes are contributing to the redefinition of the role of PSM in contemporary media systems. The study draws on a comparative analysis of five public service operators – British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC, the United Kingdom), RTÉ (Ireland), RTBF (Belgium), Radiotelevisión Española (RTVE, Spain),and RTP (Portugal) – supported by semi-structured interviews with key institutional actors and a systematic review of strategic reports, concession contracts and regulatory documents produced between 2018 and 2025. The findings reveal that, despite national specificities, several convergent trends are emerging, including the growing importance of digital platforms, the reorganization of production structures into convergent and cross-media models, and the redefinition of public service missions in a media environment shaped by platformization and intensified informational competition. The article argues that digital transformation does not diminish the relevance of PSM; on the contrary, it reinforces their importance as critical infrastructures for trustworthy information, cultural diversity and democratic cohesion.

item.title: Guardians of the cyberverse: Dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical correlates of user engagement against misogynist digital hate
item.dc:creator: Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
New Media & Society · Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Online harassment, Digital misogyny, Content moderation, Empathic anger

As digital misogyny remains widespread, user intervention is an essential complement to lenient platform governance. Yet, willingness to intervene varies considerably across individuals and cultural contexts. In a cross-national survey conducted in Austria ( n = 791), France ( n = 800), Hungary ( n = 775), and Sweden ( n = 785), we examine how dispositional, attitudinal, and autobiographical characteristics relate to users’ direct and indirect intervention and support for moderation. Empathic anger consistently emerged as the strongest positive predictor of all three outcomes across countries. Perspective-taking, online self-presentation, and victimization experiences showed meaningful positive associations with intervention, while misogynist attitudes were inconsistently related. Toxic disinhibition showed a dual pattern, negatively associated with moderation support but positively associated with direct intervention across all countries, suggesting its potential to be cleverly repurposed toward counterspeech. These findings underscore the importance of emotionally activating literacy programs and highlight the need for culturally sensitive intervention models.

item.title: Participatory journalism in practice: Assessing interactivity and citizen contributions in newsrooms
item.dc:creator: Adelino Cunha
item.description:
Journalism · Adelino Cunha

Topics: Journalism, Digital journalism, News production, Social media engagement

Digital news organisations offer audiences multiple opportunities to comment, share, submit information, and engage with journalists, but these mechanisms do not necessarily redistribute editorial authority. This article examines how interactivity enables, channels, and constrains citizen participation across the news production process. It combines a conceptual literature review, a comparative synthesis of 20 studies published between 1999 and 2025, a case analysis of The Washington Post , National Post , and The Guardian , and six written semi-structured interviews with journalists. The findings show that participation is concentrated in Access/Observation, Distribution, and Interpretation, with more limited involvement in Selection/Filtering, while Processing/Editing remains under stronger professional control. The article develops a qualitative evaluation model that distinguishes selective, communicative, and productive interactivity according to production stage, citizen agency, and implications for editorial authority. It argues that participatory journalism is best understood as managed openness: news organisations widen opportunities for citizen involvement while retaining control over the institutional core of news production, contributing to broader debates on digital participation and media power.

item.title: Negotiating exit: Career mobility and institutional status premium among young journalists in China’s mainstream media
item.dc:creator: Wanrong Li, Mingde Li
item.description:
Journalism · Wanrong Li, Mingde Li

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional identity, News production

This study examines how young journalists in China’s mainstream media negotiate career exit amid structural and technological change. Drawing on a constructivist grounded theory approach and 30 in-depth interviews with former journalists aged 35 or younger across China’s four-tier media system, we identify three interconnected concepts that shape how mobility decisions take form. First, the erosion of professional values, rooted in blurred editorial–commercial boundaries, dual-track personnel stratification, and declining social recognition, generates cumulative dissatisfaction. Second, peer comparison makes alternative career paths visible and desirable through exposure to peers’ successful transitions. Third, institutional status premium, the non-transferable symbolic capital, social recognition, and resource access tied to state-affiliated media membership, anchors journalists by raising the perceived cost of leaving. These forces do not operate uniformly. Participants from central-level media reported stronger institutional constraints and higher perceived exit costs than those from lower-level media. Older cohorts attribute greater weight to institutional status, while younger journalists, particularly the post-95 generation, place markedly less emphasis on it. Exit thus emerges not as a direct response to a single pressure but as a delayed, negotiated outcome shaped by the convergence of dissatisfaction, opportunity, and constraint. By demonstrating how these forces interact and how constraints are unevenly distributed across hierarchies and generations, the study challenges static, factor-based explanations and advances a process-oriented account of career mobility in an institutionally distinctive context.

item.title: Press freedom and media control in Pakistan: Analyzing the impact of censorship, ownership, and regulatory challenges on journalistic practices
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Ali, Hina Ali
item.description:
Journalism · Muhammad Ali, Hina Ali

Topics: Press freedom, Media systems, Journalistic practice, Media control

This study explores press freedom in Pakistan shaped by censorship, ownership, and regulatory control. Drawing on 15 semi-structured in-depth interviews with journalists and senior media professionals, the study shows that restrictions on journalism are not driven by a single mechanism but by a reinforcing system in which formal regulation (e.g., licensing and legal pressures) combines with informal coercion, surveillance, economic pressure, and organizational self-discipline. These dynamics narrow the space for independent reporting, weaken watchdog journalism, and normalize self-censorship as a professional survival strategy. Conceptually, the study argues that Pakistan’s press cannot be adequately explained through classical normative models (Developmental and Authoritarian Press) alone. It therefore advances a Hybrid Developmental–Authoritarian Press Model, capturing how developmental legitimacy narratives coexist with authoritarian enforcement tools to steer media content while preserving the appearance of pluralism.

item.title: Two Paths of Conversation: How Stories and Statistics are Associated With Community Engagement in Online Debate Surrounding Vaccine Science Skeptical Content
item.dc:creator: Han Zao Li, Inhwan Bae, Pengfei Zhao, Natalya N. Bazarova, Drew Margolin
item.description:
Communication Research · Han Zao Li, Inhwan Bae, Pengfei Zhao, Natalya N. Bazarova, Drew Margolin

Topics: Misinformation, Health communication, Social media discourse, Online communities

Statistical and narrative evidence represent two distinct ways of substantiating claims in public reasoning, but does this distinction matter for how people engage with vaccine science skeptical (VSS) content and the discursive spaces surrounding it? This study addresses this question through a large-scale, LLM-assisted observational analysis of online engagement with VSS posts and comments that support or counter such content using statistical versus narrative evidence in the Reddit community r/DebateVaccines . Building on Fisher’s distinction between rational and narrative paradigms , we theorize two paths of conversation through which evidentiary forms are associated with audience engagement with contentious vaccine discourses in a naturalistic social media setting: a rational pathway, marked by concentrated participation and corrective contestation around statistical claims and counterclaims, tending toward a single evidence-based truth “approved” by one-click reactions; and a narrative pathway, characterized by generative engagement featuring broader and more distributed participation, more discursive and generative engagement, and greater acceptance of competing viewpoints. These findings provide a springboard for theorizing evidentiary form as a key epistemic logic associated with how conversations evolve in real-world engagement with contentious, socially consequential issues such as vaccine misinformation, while informing hybrid approaches to addressing skepticism toward established vaccine science.

item.title: Constantly Connected, Differently Affected: Response Speed Shapes Parents’ and Adolescents’ Feelings of Connection
item.dc:creator: Razieh Pourafshari, Miriam Brinberg, Joseph Bayer
item.description:
Communication Research · Razieh Pourafshari, Miriam Brinberg, Joseph Bayer

Topics: Social media use, Interpersonal communication, Well-being, Communication theory

Response speed in digital communication serves as a signal of availability, yet past research has overlooked how speed expectations in specific relationships translate into social connection. This study addresses this oversight by integrating theoretical perspectives on constant connectivity and chronemics to test the implications of perceived response speed for parent-adolescent relationships. Using a 28-day dyadic daily diary design of 142 parent-adolescent dyads, we examined how one’s own and one’s partner’s perceived response speed were associated with feelings of connection. Results revealed asymmetric and interdependent patterns. Faster response speed perceptions predicted greater connection, but these associations were more pronounced for parents. Additionally, parents’ perceptions of adolescents’ response speed predicted adolescents’ feelings of connection. These findings indicate that response speed perceptions can act as a mechanism that links connectivity to social connection in everyday life, but this depends on relational role.

item.title: Subversive memory work: Reworking journalism and its digital archives to contest dominant memory regimes
item.dc:creator: Rahoof Kaliyarakath
item.description:
Journalism · Rahoof Kaliyarakath

Topics: Journalism, Digital archives, Media memory, Journalistic practice

Media scholarship has long established journalism as a form of memory work. Yet conventional journalistic practices, particularly elite-centered sourcing and dominant news values, privilege certain actors and experiences while marginalizing others, producing dominant memory regimes. Drawing on a qualitative case study of the People’s Archive of Rural India (PARI), this study examines how dominant memory regimes can be contested from within journalism. It develops subversive memory work as a conceptual framework organized around two domains of mnemonic power, production and access. The framework identifies four interrelated dimensions, namely everyday witnessing, structural witnessing, cultural witnessing, and accessible counter-memory infrastructure. Together, these dimensions capture journalistic and archival practices that bring the lives, experiences, and forms of knowledge of ordinary people and historically marginalized communities into the journalistic record and make them available for future access. The study argues that subversive memory work contests dominant memory regimes by reworking both journalistic production and archiving practices.

item.title: Centralized hashtags, embedded discourse: Two structural logics of youth climate activism on social media
item.dc:creator: Yuzhe Zhu, Gustavo Cardoso
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Yuzhe Zhu, Gustavo Cardoso

Topics: Social media activism, Climate change communication, Digital activism, Social media analysis

Youth-led climate action increasingly unfolds on digital platforms, where hashtags structurally connect issues, actors, and publics. Using hashtag co-occurrence data (2022–2024) from prominent youth climate activists on X and Portuguese youth climate activists on Instagram, this study applies link community analysis, which captures overlapping multi-membership structures that node-based clustering obscures. Two contrasting structural logics emerge. The international network exhibits a centralized configuration in which core climate hashtags such as #FridaysForFuture and #Peoplenotprofit occupy bridging positions across issue communities, so that visibility and structural centrality closely align. The Portuguese network displays a more horizontal configuration in which climate-related hashtags co-occur with feminism, education, domestic politics, and art-based activism, embedding climate discourse within everyday publics. Digital climate publics take shape as relational structures produced through patterns of hashtag overlap and cross-issue connectivity.

item.title: Victim identity and political consequentiality: Framing migrant and citizen deaths in the Greek press
item.dc:creator: Nikolaos Lampas, Vasileios Vlaseros
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Nikolaos Lampas, Vasileios Vlaseros

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Political communication, Journalism

Why do mass-fatality events with comparable human tolls generate unequal political resonance? This article examines Greek newspaper coverage of two major 2023 tragedies, the Tempi train crash and the Pylos shipwreck, to assess how victim identity shapes evaluative framing, responsibility attribution, and political consequentiality. Drawing on a within-country comparison of three ideologically distinct newspapers, the study analyses how each event was narrated, politicized, and sustained over time. The findings show that, although both tragedies were covered within a broadly negative register, Tempi generated denser evaluative language, more direct attribution of responsibility, and more durable integration into debates over governance and institutional accountability. By contrast, Pylos was more frequently framed through humanitarian, administrative, or border-management narratives and declined more rapidly after the initial news cycle. These differences were patterned rather than categorical and persisted across outlets. The article argues that routine journalistic framing practices help determine not only how tragedy is represented, but whether it becomes politically consequential as a sustained object of public accountability.

item.title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
item.dc:creator: Atte Oksanen, Teo Keipi, Moona Heiskari, Iina Savolainen
item.description:
New Media & Society · Atte Oksanen, Teo Keipi, Moona Heiskari, Iina Savolainen

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Well-being, Professional identity, Digital transformation

Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

item.title: Institutional sentinel: Journalistic role performance and the defense of media autonomy under democratic threat
item.dc:creator: Vytautas Valentinavičius
item.description:
Journalism · Vytautas Valentinavičius

Topics: Journalistic role performance, Media autonomy, Public service media, Press freedom

This article develops the concept of the institutional sentinel to explain how journalists may temporarily reconfigure professional role performance when the institutional conditions of independent reporting become objects of political contestation. Existing debates on journalism under democratic strain often frame departures from conventional objectivity as either activism or part of a moral turn. Such binaries overlook a more specific form of intervention: the public defense of governance arrangements, editorial autonomy, and organizational safeguards that enable impartial reporting. The institutional sentinel is defined as a situationally activated role-performance logic in which journalists collectively shift from monitorial observation to defending these conditions when they are publicly framed as being under procedural threat. The article is conceptual and uses the 2025–2026 conflict surrounding Lithuania’s public broadcaster, LRT, as a revelatory vignette. The vignette clarifies three elements: activation under perceived procedural threat within a context shaped by threat fusion; boundedness, expressed through temporariness, role transparency, object specificity, and reversibility; and a defensive paradox whereby institutional self-defense may protect autonomy while exposing journalism to accusations of bias, self-interest, or partisanship. The article offers a mid-range conceptual tool and develops scope conditions and propositions for comparative research on media autonomy, legitimacy, and professional boundary work.

item.title: What Makes Child Harm Newsworthy? Event Characteristics, Victim Characteristics, and Media Attention
item.dc:creator: Тернов Николай Максимович, Kuralay A. Mukhambetova, Z.T. Abetova
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Тернов Николай Максимович, Kuralay A. Mukhambetova, Z.T. Abetova

Topics: News values, News coverage, Media attention, Journalism studies

Media coverage shapes public understanding of social problems, yet harmful events receive uneven attention even when they involve children. This study examines factors shaping media visibility of child harm in Kazakhstan. Using a corpus of more than 230,000 Telegram news posts (2020–2025), we identify 1,571 incidents involving harm to children and estimate negative binomial regression models to test explanations derived from news values and ideal victim theory. Results show that event characteristics predict media attention more strongly than victim characteristics. Fatal interpersonal violence receives more coverage, while systemic failures receive less. Victim age and gender are not significant predictors.

item.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on journalism: How media trust and attitudes toward journalists shape acceptance, trust, willingness to pay for AI news, and support for replacing journalists
item.dc:creator: Manuel Goyanes, Marína Urbániková, Beatriz Jordá
item.description:
Journalism · Manuel Goyanes, Marína Urbániková, Beatriz Jordá

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Media trust, Journalism, Audience perception

Although AI is advancing rapidly in many fields, its use in journalism is especially significant, as journalism shapes public opinion and fosters democratic discourse. Artificial intelligence (AI), in particular, has attracted attention for its potential to greatly enhance journalists’ work, but also raises concerns about ethics and job displacement. However, previous research has largely overlooked the public’s perspective on AI, even though understanding these views is crucial for predicting future consumption patterns. This study addresses this gap using data from cross-sectional surveys in Spain ( N = 2337) and Germany ( N = 2213), revealing cautious public attitudes toward AI in journalism. In both countries, acceptance of AI in journalism, trust in its output, willingness to pay for it, and acceptance of AI replacing human journalists are moderate to low. Favorable attitudes toward human journalists positively influence views of AI in journalism, while trust in the media shows a mixed effect. Overall, the findings suggest that public attitudes toward AI in journalism align with broader views on AI, with individual perceptions of AI being a stronger determinant than opinions on media and journalists.

item.title: Uniformity, diversity, and memetics: Editorial adaptation in Civil War–era American journalism
item.dc:creator: Zef M. Segal, Menahem Blondheim
item.description:
Journalism · Zef M. Segal, Menahem Blondheim

Topics: Journalistic practice, News production, News media, Media systems

This article examines how U.S. newspapers during the Civil War circulated shared news content while persistently reshaping it, revealing a dynamic interplay between national integration and local differentiation in nineteenth-century American journalism. While scholarship has emphasized the homogenizing effects of postal exchanges and telegraphic wire services, this study shows that diversity in news presentation was a routine and structured feature of wartime journalism. Drawing on a close comparison of twenty-six matched articles published in the Chicago Tribune and the Alexandria Gazette, the article uses the lens of journalistic memetics to distinguish between uniform transmission and patterned editorial adaptation. The analysis identifies six recurring forms of editorial intervention: typographic adjustment, lexical change, selective omission, reordering, shifts in placement and headlines, and factual divergence. Through these interventions, shared items were adapted to local audiences, material constraints, and sectional political environments. Using memetics as a heuristic for distinguishing replication from adaptation, the article contributes to journalism studies by reframing reprinting not as passive reproduction but as an active process of journalistic transformation. It argues that uniform infrastructures of distribution did not eliminate editorial diversity; rather, they depended on persistent local adaptation as a condition of news circulation.

item.title: Beyond Seamlessness: Mobile AI and Situated Sense-Making
item.dc:creator: Thilo von Pape
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Thilo von Pape

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Mobile media, Human-computer interaction, Communication theory

This commentary explores what it means for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to become mobile, as interaction shifts from screen-bound querying to AI participation in the flow of everyday situations. Rather than framing this shift in terms of access or use, it approaches mobile AI through situated sense-making, understood here in terms of the constitution of sense through ongoing activities, embodied cues, social coordination, and mobile communication affordances as AI becomes part of the situation. Starting from a café interaction staged in a promotional video for a future AI device, the commentary confronts corporate claims of seamless interaction with theoretical accounts of situated sense-making. Drawing on mobile communication studies and human–machine communication (HMC), it argues that mobile AI requires a specification of sense-making as HMC's central boundary object: not only as mutual interpretation between users and interfaces but also as a process embedded in ongoing activities and interactions. The commentary develops this argument through three interrelated aspects of situated sense-making—coordination, distribution, and stabilization—showing how mobile AI may reshape participation, redistribute epistemic authority, and steer relevance toward either shared problematization or premature closure. It thereby advances an approach to analyzing and designing embodied AI that foregrounds visible coordination, responsive alignment, and stabilization that remains open to collective deliberation.

item.title: “I’m Here to Work and Not to Call”: Blue-Collar Workers Navigating Interruptions by Mobile Devices
item.dc:creator: Floor Fiers
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Floor Fiers

Topics: Mobile communication, Workplace interruptions, Blue-collar workers, Organizational communication

In blue-collar work, such as construction and landscaping, mobile devices allow for communication across dispersed workplaces while posing risks to worker outcomes, including physical safety. When mobile devices interrupt workers, they are tasked with making rapid decisions about how to respond. This study examines how blue-collar workers experience and navigate interruptions by mobile communication technologies. Based on 46 semi-structured interviews nested in a phone survey of employees of a blue-collar company in the Netherlands, results reveal that when interrupted by their mobile devices, workers engage in a complex negotiation process in which they weigh a myriad of contextual factors and consider different response options. Participants describe three general strategies to approach these negotiations: devising rules to guide their choices, taking preventative measures to limit the choices they need to make, and structurally deprioritizing mobile communication altogether. Ultimately, the study highlights that managing interruptions in high-risk environments constitutes a complex skill, one that demands more scholarly and managerial attention.

item.title: Psycho-social risk and protective factors associated with resilience in journalism
item.dc:creator: Маријана Марковиќ, Елеонора Серафимовска
item.description:
Journalism · Маријана Марковиќ, Елеонора Серафимовска

Topics: Journalism, Well-being, Mental health, Political communication

The polarized socio-political context is a defining feature of Macedonian society, marked by challenges such as limited transparency in political and media institutions, pressure on journalists, disinformation, and self-censorship. Reporting under such prolonged and complex conditions places considerable demands on journalists’ coping capacities and resilience. This study examines the relationship between psychosocial risk factors in the work environment and resilience among journalists in Macedonia. A field survey was conducted between March and June 2025 using the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ-III) to assess psychosocial risk factors and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-25) to measure resilience. The findings suggest that journalists identify job insecurity, organizational justice, horizontal trust, work-life conflict, quality of leadership, and emotional demands as key psychosocial risk factors. The results further indicate a moderately high level of resilience, suggesting that journalists are generally able to cope with demanding working conditions, although not without strain. Correlation analysis reveals that resilience is positively associated with protective work-related factors, including meaning of work, role clarity, possibilities for development, influence at work, and sense of community, while showing a significant negative association with job insecurity. Overall, the findings suggest that journalists’ resilience is strengthened by supportive organizational conditions and weakened by uncertainty and insecurity in the work environment. The study underscores the need to reduce psychosocial risks and enhance supportive and fair working conditions in order to sustain journalists’ resilience in the Macedonian socio-political context.

item.title: The hierarchy of humanization: A theory of victim visibility in news narratives
item.dc:creator: Maurice N. Emelu, Chika Nwugo, Regina Tuma, Sean Sims, Mariah Moulds, Elijah Williams, Felipe Covarrubias
item.description:
Journalism · Maurice N. Emelu, Chika Nwugo, Regina Tuma, Sean Sims, Mariah Moulds, Elijah Williams, Felipe Covarrubias

Topics: News framing, Gender representation, Journalism, Media representation

Journalism frames events and distributes human recognition in public discourse, yet little is known about how narrative attention is allocated among individuals within the same event. This study introduces Victim Visibility Theory (VVT), conceptualizing news stories as systems of narrative allocation in which victims receive unequal levels of humanization. Drawing on a content analysis of 433 articles from four U.S. elite newspapers covering 52 victims across four mass shootings, it examines how identity cues, symbolic capital, and structural narrative prominence shape representation. The findings show that humanization is allocated at two levels: first between events, where whole tragedies are humanized unequally, and then within events, where editorial placement provides a second-order layer of differentiation. Victims granted headline and lead placement consistently receive expanded interpretive development, while identity attributes and symbolic capital show limited, inconsistent effects. This two-level hierarchy of humanization repositions framing in a broader model of narrative visibility and informs more equitable journalistic practice.

item.title: The False Will Set You Free: How Lower Courts Have Translated the Supreme Court’s Latest Falsity Doctrine into Practice
item.dc:creator: Robert L. Kerr
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Robert L. Kerr

Topics: Misinformation, Press freedom, Communication theory, Content moderation

This study provides the first descriptive mapping of the impact of the First Amendment’s rationale for advancing truth-seeking being extended counter-intuitively to provide greater protection for intentional falsehoods. Scholarly concerns over the Supreme Court’s Alvarez ruling focused on potentially creating a doctrinal vacuum of limited guidance. The study found lower courts reflected more clarity of guidance when cases involved the sorts of historically unprotected categories of false expression targeting harm beyond falsity—but considerably less so in other types of cases where it was often “not entirely clear what level of scrutiny is appropriate for laws that criminalize lying.”

item.title: Stories that Make Hawks? Digital News-Based User-Generated Content and Foreign Policy Orientations Among China’s Generation Z
item.dc:creator: Yang Li, Ying Hooi Khoo, Siti Ezaleila Mustafa
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Yang Li, Ying Hooi Khoo, Siti Ezaleila Mustafa

Topics: Social media, User-generated content, Narrative persuasion, Political communication

This study examines the relationships between exposure to news-based user-generated content on Bilibili and Chinese Generation Z’s support for hawkish foreign policies. Guided by the Narrative Policy Framework, a survey ( N = 688) shows that self-reported exposure to villain, hero, and mixed narrative strategies is positively associated with hawkish orientations, both directly and indirectly through national pride and national humiliation. These findings suggest that, within the highly performative and affectively embedded dynamics of social media, nonofficial actors may rely on dramatized storytelling and serve as a nonnegligible component of the broader rise of hawkishness within Chinese youth communities.

item.title: Human Imagery and Psychological Reactance in Persuasive Health Messages
item.dc:creator: Chelsea L. Ratcliff, Helen M. Lillie, Manusheela Pokharel, Jakob D. Jensen, Doris E. Acheme, Benjamin Sam-Paintsil
item.description:
Communication Research · Chelsea L. Ratcliff, Helen M. Lillie, Manusheela Pokharel, Jakob D. Jensen, Doris E. Acheme, Benjamin Sam-Paintsil

Topics: Psychological reactance, Persuasion, Health communication, Message effects

Although mass-mediated persuasive messages often feature images of people, their impacts are surprisingly understudied. We tested whether attributes of human imagery influence psychological reactance to a health promotion PSA, either alone or combined with language style. Participants ( N = 1,100) viewed a message promoting sun safety that contained a forceful (vs. courteous) appeal and featured a model with forceful (vs. neutral) body language. The model’s physical characteristics (gender and skin tone) also varied. Both forceful text and forceful body language indirectly lowered protective behavioral intentions via reactance, and male-model messages had this effect for female participants. Our findings demonstrate the potential for features of human imagery to inadvertently hinder persuasion. Study results also highlight the value in measuring perceived visual freedom threat alongside traditional reactance measures. We discuss implications for reactance theory and measurement and highlight important directions for research on reactance to visuals.

item.title: Texting for Connection in an “Always-On” Society: Roles of Content, Availability Pressure, and Emotional Fatigue
item.dc:creator: David de Segovia Vicente, Mariek Vanden Abeele, Kyle Van Gaeveren, Stephen Lee Murphy, Jeffrey A. Hall
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · David de Segovia Vicente, Mariek Vanden Abeele, Kyle Van Gaeveren, Stephen Lee Murphy, Jeffrey A. Hall

Topics: Computer-mediated communication, Interpersonal communication, Smartphone use, Well-being

Texting is the most ubiquitous form of computer-mediated communication, but its ability to satisfy relational needs in an always-on society remains under scrutiny. This study examines how message content and psychological context—specifically emotional fatigue and availability pressure—determine the relational value of texting. Analyzing 5,821 ecological momentary assessments from 112 adults, the results reveal that while texting and offline interactions positively predict connectedness, offline interactions demonstrate a meaningfully stronger effect. Within the context of texting, meaningful and affectionate interactions are associated with high levels of connectedness compared with those of small talk or practical exchanges, supporting the hierarchy of communication episodes proposed by communicate bond belong theory. Notably, neither emotional fatigue nor availability pressure significantly influences the association between texting and connectedness. These findings highlight that the relational benefits of texting are resilient to emotional fatigue and availability pressure and primarily depend on the nature of the content instead of users' psychological context.

item.title: Compressed Time, Narrow Space: The Visual-Temporal Aesthetics of Mobile Microdrama on ReelShort
item.dc:creator: Seda Aktaş
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Seda Aktaş

Topics: Short-form video, Digital media, Visual communication, Mobile media

The widespread adoption of digital platforms and mobile devices has significantly transformed audiovisual storytelling. Short-form mobile microdramas represent not only a new mode of distribution but also a narrative form that reorganizes cinematic time and space. While previous research has primarily focused on platform economies, audience engagement, and algorithmic circulation, the visual-temporal organization of mobile microdramas has received comparatively little attention from the perspective of quantitative film analysis. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how mobile microdramas reorganize cinematic form through temporal compression and spatial narrowing. A quantitative formal analysis was conducted on the first episodes of 10 ReelShort series representing different narrative tropes. The analysis examined average shot length (ASL), editing rhythm, shots per minute, shot-scale distribution, and the use of establishing shots. Shot boundaries were automatically identified using Adobe Premiere Pro's Scene Edit Detection tool, while shot scales and spatial indicators were analysed through qualitative coding. The findings show that an exceptionally short ASL of 2.31 s, together with the predominance of medium shots and the limited use of full/long shots and establishing shots, minimizes spatial exposition while privileging character-centred compositions and producing a dense visual rhythm optimized for smartphone viewing. The results suggest that ReelShort reorganizes cinematic form by simultaneously compressing cinematic time and narrowing cinematic space, extending long-term stylistic tendencies in film history while adapting them to the perceptual and technological conditions of vertically oriented mobile media.

item.title: Defensive avoidance: How intimidating, belief-incongruent, and repetitive news disengages social media users from news
item.dc:creator: Maliha Khanam, Md. Sayeed Al-Zaman
item.description:
Journalism · Maliha Khanam, Md. Sayeed Al-Zaman

Topics: News avoidance, Social media, Selective exposure, Digital media

Social media has become a key news source worldwide, transforming how people access and consume news. Despite easy access and availability of news, many users gradually tend to disengage from news consumption. Research indicates that factors such as overload and fatigue contribute to this trend, while some psychological mechanisms remain less understood, especially in non-Western contexts. To address this, we surveyed 417 Bangladeshi social media users who consume news and tested four hypotheses. Our multiple regression analysis revealed that belief-based selective avoidance, perceived threat, and news redundancy are positively associated with news avoidance, with perceived threat being the strongest factor (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). News redundancy (β = 0.16, p = 0.001) and belief-based selective avoidance (β = 0.10, p = 0.039) also play significant roles. Trust showed a weaker, nonsignificant effect (β = −0.04, p = 0.383). These results indicate that news avoidance reflects selective disengagement from news perceived as threatening, repetitive, or belief-incongruent. By focusing on Bangladesh, this study broadens research on social media news avoidance to the Global South. Exploring some tentative steps for news outlets, such as promoting constructive journalism and reviewing digital-friendly editorial policies, could help reduce news avoidance. Limitations remain in sampling, among others.

item.title: Public reactions on TikTok: Emotional dynamics in comments to the president of Romania's posts
item.dc:creator: Tănase Tasențe, Cristina-Dana Popescu
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Tănase Tasențe, Cristina-Dana Popescu

Topics: TikTok, Political communication, Sentiment analysis, Social media discourse

This article examines how TikTok structures the emotional dynamics of presidential communication during the initial months of a mandate, focusing on the official account of the President of Romania. Drawing on 44 TikTok posts and 29,756 unique public comments recorded between 26 May and 27 October 2025, the study combines multilingual transformer-based sentiment analysis, change-point analysis and co-commenting network analysis. After deduplication and temporal filtering, 21,654 comments were classified. The results show a positive plurality rather than a uniformly positive baseline, alongside issue-specific negativity around economic governance, justice and public safety, security, Moldova and democratic legitimacy. Validation sensitivity checks caution against strong comment-level claims, whilst a bipartite null model shows that much co-commenting density is expected from shared participation in viral threads. TikTok is therefore interpreted as a high-co-presence environment in which episodic affective pressure emerges around salient political themes.

item.title: Heterogeneities of Smartphone Use Among Chinese Urban Older Adults: A Life Course Approach
item.dc:creator: Lu Chen, Miaoting Cheng
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Lu Chen, Miaoting Cheng

Topics: Smartphone use, Older adults, Life course, Digital inequality

Drawing on a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interview data, this research adopts a life course perspective to examine how Chinese urban older adults adjust their smartphone use in response to significant life events across later life. The findings reveal that multi-level life events foster a dynamic continuum of (dis)connection. At the same time, adaptive and maladaptive use patterns coexist among Chinese urban older adults, demonstrating heterogeneity in their smartphone use. By proposing a shift from an age-as-variable approach to an aging-as-process approach, this study emphasizes older adults’ contextualized (dis)connectivity situated within life course transitions and trajectories, which reflects a negotiation between individual agency and socio-technical structures.

item.title: Platformed affective withdrawal: Quiet quitting and the refusal of gendered emotional labour on TikTok
item.dc:creator: Aybüke KAPLAN
item.description:
New Media & Society · Aybüke KAPLAN

Topics: Short-form video, TikTok, Digital labor, Platform studies

This article examines #quietquitting on TikTok as a platform-mediated articulation of gendered affective withdrawal. While organisational research interprets quiet quitting as reduced discretionary effort or declining work engagement, this study examines how quiet quitting is articulated as a digitally circulated refusal of feminised emotional labour. Drawing on feminist theories of affective labour and critical platform studies, the analysis explores how workers renegotiate expectations of emotional availability within algorithmically structured visibility regimes. The study is based on a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods analysis of 586 TikTok videos shared under #quietquitting between 2020 and 2026. Combining thematic discourse analysis with descriptive engagement indicators, the findings show that creators frequently frame quiet quitting as a refusal of unpaid relational mediation, emotional management, and workplace care. The article introduces the concept of platformed affective withdrawal to explain how narratives of workplace disengagement circulate through algorithmic visibility systems that amplify and individualise gendered labour inequalities.

item.title: Praise, rent, and the platform: Substack and the enclosure of blog culture
item.dc:creator: Will Riley
item.description:
New Media & Society · Will Riley

Topics: Platform studies, Platformization, Digital labour, Social media platforms

This article situates Substack within the platformisation of blogging and the enclosure of cultural production within proprietary infrastructures. Tracing the genealogy of blogging as a decentralised practice that carried within it the seeds of citizen journalism and informal intellectual life, I argue that Substack does not restore an apparently lost cultural practice but renegotiates and interpolates blogging into a platformised logic. Framed as a return to independent, writer-led publishing, Substack instead, as I argue, renders free-labour interaction as a source of rent. I analyse the rhetoric and revolving discourse around Substack’s internal curatorial project, ‘The Substack Post’. Drawing on Jodi Dean’s account of blogs as displaced mediators alongside theories of digital labour and platform capitalism, and approaching Substack as a simultaneously platformised and infrastructuralised formation, I argue that praise operates as a platform-specific form of commodity fetishism, animating the platform while obscuring the labour relations that sustain it.

item.title: Reconfiguring repression: Violence against journalists in Indonesia under democratic backsliding (2014–2025)
item.dc:creator: Wisnu Prasetya Utomo
item.description:
Journalism · Wisnu Prasetya Utomo

Topics: Press freedom, Journalism, Political communication, Digital harassment

Violence against journalists in Indonesia has been reconfigured as a broader system of repression under democratic backsliding. This article examines how repression adapts under such conditions by conceptualizing violence as authoritarian innovation. Repression is redistributed across forms, perpetrators, and targets, preserving deniability while maintaining disciplinary effects. Analyzing 780 documented incidents (2014–2025) from the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI), the study codes violence across forms (physical, digital, legal, obstruction), perpetrators (state actors, non-state actors, unknown), and targets (individual journalists, media organizations). The analysis traces violence’s longitudinal reconfiguration under democratic backsliding. Three patterns emerge. First, physical attacks persist but increasingly coexist with digital harassment and obstruction. Second, perpetrator attribution becomes increasingly opaque, with unknown actors responsible for more incidents than police or non-state actors by 2025. Third, attacks targeting media organizations rise sixfold. The findings extend authoritarian innovation and press freedom scholarship, revealing how repression adapts temporally through accumulation and layering.

item.title: Quietly taking sides: The machine habitus and metaphorical framing in human and LLM-generated news
item.dc:creator: Xiaoshuang Guo
item.description:
Journalism · Xiaoshuang Guo

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Generative AI, Large Language Models, Journalistic practice

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft the news. These systems may frame the news differently from human journalists. In particular, it remains less understood how they handle metaphor, a potent framing tool in news discourse. Following Bourdieu’s field theory, we compare LLMs’ metaphorical framing with the journalistic habitus of human reporting in two studies of German news on Chinese investment spanning a quarter century (with 2975 metaphors from human journalism and 1924 from LLM-generated news writing), and conduct a prompting experiment across four instructions and three recent LLMs (DeepSeek V4, GPT-5.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) with 4877 metaphors. We find that compared to journalists that favored deliberate, evaluatively charged figurative expressions, the LLM-generated news was conventional by default, framing investment as a procedural, depoliticized process. We regard this disposition as a “machine habitus”. It proved durable across prompted years and model versions, bound to a closed set of source domains, and generative , varying under instruction only within that set. Its conceptual sources and deliberateness moved sharply with the prompt, yet showed little variation across LLMs, while its evaluative orientation tracked the prompt, with only weak differences by model origin. Across two versions of LLMs, the disposition proved more durable than the volume of metaphor it governs: the newer LLMs wrote more figuratively yet remained conflict-averse. The study contributes to debates on automation, framing, and accountability in journalism.

item.title: A genealogy of conceptual confusion: Epistemological fault lines across media-ritual concepts
item.dc:creator: Hung-Yen Hsu
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Hung-Yen Hsu

Topics: Communication theory, Media effects, Mediatization, Communication science

Research on media–ritual intersections deploys seven concepts: media events, media rituals, mediatized rituals, media ritualization, ritual mediatization, ritual media, and ritualized media. Their overlap generates unmarked substitution between analytically divergent registers. The slippage is a structural consequence of three epistemological tributaries (Durkheimian social theory, Carey's ritual view, and mediatization theory), each foregrounding a different dimension of the same phenomena. Genealogical analysis diagnoses four confusions: process conflated with product, unmarked shifting among power paradigms, materiality–practice divergence, and directional inversion. Three fault lines (integration vs. domination, process vs. structure, exceptional vs. everyday) constitute a meta-theoretical framework. The article advances positioned conceptual deployment: researchers specify their coordinates along all three dimensions. The seven concepts serve as a diagnostic case: concept use in communication research presupposes epistemological commitments, marked or not. An under-theorized intersection, mediatized ritualization, is advanced as a provisional theoretical proposition about how platform architectures may reshape ritualized media practice.

item.title: Finding Love in the Black Box: Algorithm Awareness on Dating Apps
item.dc:creator: Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans

Topics: Online dating, Algorithm awareness, Trust, Human-computer interaction

Most dating apps use algorithms to match users to one another, but are not fully transparent about how their recommender systems work. In turn, users have varying degrees of awareness of matching algorithms. Unfortunately, little is known about how awareness of algorithmic functioning relates to online dating. This research examined the relationship between algorithm awareness, trust in algorithms, and satisfaction with the quality of matches. A survey was conducted among 500 users of the Dutch dating app Breeze, presented to respondents within the app itself. Relationships were estimated with structural equation modeling. Higher algorithm awareness was associated with more trust in algorithms, which positively related to satisfaction with the quality of matches. This mediated association between awareness and satisfaction with matches suggested that awareness of matching algorithms is associated with better outcomes of dating app use. This research contributes to the limited literature on human-algorithm interaction on dating apps. Overall, the results suggest that algorithm awareness may be a relevant part of the online dating experience.

item.title: Not only correcting lies. Analysis of interventionist strategies in news articles dealing with misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic in the Netherlands
item.dc:creator: David Blanco‐Herrero, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer, Bas van den Putte
item.description:
Journalism · David Blanco‐Herrero, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer, Bas van den Putte

Topics: Misinformation, Journalistic roles, Health communication, COVID-19 pandemic

During crises, when falsehoods often spread faster than facts, journalists face the challenge of deciding how to fight misinformation without amplifying its reach. This study focuses on Dutch journalists who addressed pandemic-related misinformation during the COVID-19 crisis (January 2020–May 2023), distinguishing between actively interventionist strategies (correction and prebunking) and more detached approaches. Drawing on a content analysis of 698 news articles, it investigates the use of actively interventionist strategies, and their variation across pandemic phases and in their use of expert sources. Findings show that 14.2% of articles adopted actively interventionist roles, with corrections being more common than prebunking. Such strategies were more frequent during the initial uncertain phase of the pandemic and during vaccine rollouts. Articles using these strategies relied on a greater number and diversity of sources, especially academic, governmental, and health-related. The results highlight a cautious engagement by journalists in actively countering misinformation, favoring a more detached reporting. Overall, the study advances the understanding of journalistic role performance in health crises and the interplay between journalism practice and misinformation management.

item.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
item.dc:creator: Linda Li, Helen Margetts
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Linda Li, Helen Margetts

Topics: Social bots, Social media activism, Digital activism, Computational text analysis

Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

item.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
item.dc:creator: Moreno Mancosu, Mario Quaranta, Fabio Torreggiani
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Moreno Mancosu, Mario Quaranta, Fabio Torreggiani

Topics: Social media use, Smartphone use, Digital trace data, Facebook

Social media platforms structure the ways in which billions of citizens access information. Nevertheless, to assess social media time use, most research relies on limited data sources, such as self-reported survey measures or behavioral data from single platforms or convenience samples. Using 6 weeks of passive metering of smartphone and computer activity from a quota sample of Italian adults (18–70, n = 1,457), this study provides a behaviorally measured account of platform-specific social media use across the adult population. We quantify time allocation across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Twitter/X and examine how use varies by sociodemographic factors. Results show that Facebook and YouTube dominate everyday social media time, accounting for nearly three-quarters of consumption, while Instagram attracts comparable average time from a narrower user base, and TikTok shows concentrated usage among younger adopters. Twitter/X occupies a marginal niche. Use is overwhelmingly app-based (>90%), a pattern that browser-based measurement cannot capture. Age is the strongest demographic predictor: Gen Z concentrates attention on Instagram and TikTok, while older cohorts favor Facebook; YouTube shows weak demographic patterning. Gender and education are consistent secondary predictors: women devote more time to Facebook, Instagram, and social media overall, and higher education is associated with lower aggregate use and a smaller share on Facebook and TikTok. Employment and income show null effects. Together, these behavioral, cross-platform figures provide a more accurate basis for weighting platforms by their actual audiences than self-reported or single-platform evidence allows.

item.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
item.dc:creator: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler‐Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, SARA BINZER HOBOLT, Claes H. de Vreese
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler‐Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, SARA BINZER HOBOLT, Claes H. de Vreese

Topics: AI-generated content, Generative AI, Misinformation, Information credibility

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) dramatically lowers the costs of creating high-quality, realistic images, allowing a wider range of actors to create and distribute such content on, for instance, social media. A core concern is that easy-to-use generative AI tools can be misused for manipulation through misinformation and microtargeted persuasive material. However, we still need more contextual nuance to a fundamental question: To what degree can people discern photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images? In a preregistered survey experiment, we find that, on average, people are not substantially better than chance at discerning AI-generated images from authentic images, regardless of the context of the image. While younger people, highly analytical-thinking individuals, and experienced users of generative AI have better discernment abilities, no demographic group other than young individuals (<25) performs substantially better than chance. Contrary to our expectation, we do not find that people’s confidence in their discernment abilities varies depending on the context of the image. As generative AI technology likely advances and the realism of AI-generated images continues to improve, these findings are concerning, as people already struggle to discern between AI-generated and authentic images, even in an experiment where they have been primed and are assessing images of relatively low quality.

item.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
item.dc:creator: Amanda M. McLeroy, Tiera Tanksley
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Amanda M. McLeroy, Tiera Tanksley

Topics: Adolescent mental health, Social media algorithms, Algorithmic curation, Mental health

This study explores the pervasive presence of racially traumatic content (RTC) on social media and its profound impact on the mental well-being of Black youth. Utilizing ethnographic content analysis and grounded in critical race technology theory (CRTT), the research identifies key manifestations of RTC, including Black death, digital harassment, deepfakes, and war content. Social media’s algorithmic structures amplify RTC, perpetuating systemic anti-Black racism while exposing Black youth to vicarious trauma, anxiety, and depression. Despite these challenges, social media platforms also provide spaces for activism and community-building. Black youth use these digital arenas to engage in social justice narratives, find solidarity, and develop coping strategies. The findings emphasize the critical roles of educators and counselors in mitigating the adverse effects of RTC by fostering media literacy, digital resilience, and culturally responsive mental health support. This research contributes to evidence-based interventions aimed at empowering Black youth to navigate digital spaces safely, advocate for systemic change, and thrive in an equitable and inclusive online environment.

item.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
item.dc:creator: Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Ochiai Yoichi
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Ochiai Yoichi

Topics: Social networks, Social media, Online communities, Digital media

The Ainu are Indigenous people living primarily in Japan. As they have recently adopted social media, and network-based analyses of First Nations cultural manifestations are uncommon, this study drew on Indigenous and social network frameworks to examine creative networks in the virtual Mosir (the world as viewed by the Ainu). Our objective was to clarify the types of collaborators, their cooperation patterns and relationships relevant to producing Ainu-related YouTube videos. Three YouTube lists of 428 videos were utilised in this study. Publicly available data were downloaded using a YouTube Application Programming Interface (API). The videos were watched and classified, including anonymised data on collaborators. The relationships of the collaborators were quantified and mapped, network measurements were calculated and collaborator clusters were examined. The most frequent types of collaborators were individuals and communities. We also observed that individuals moderately affected network clustering ( p = .002). Furthermore, individuals were somewhat correlated with the average number of ties ( p = .004) and the bridging of clusters through betweenness ( p = .006), with Japanese male celebrities and Ainu people, particularly Ainu women, showing high centrality. As Indigenous rights advance internationally, the virtual Mosir shows how crucial it is for First Nations to participate in multimedia production processes, particularly if such productions are available on social media. Indigenous network frameworks were highly compatible with network analysis, allowing for a more comprehensive overview of Indigenous production processes. This can enhance the multiple knowledges of First Nations, while fostering accountability and reciprocity of their allies.

item.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
item.dc:creator: Sara Van Bruyssel
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Sara Van Bruyssel

Topics: Digital well-being, Digital media, Well-being, Privacy

Although always-on connectivity affords autonomy, it also creates dependencies on digital devices. Digital disconnection has emerged as a countermovement, with people seeking ‘authentic’ offline reconnection under the discourse of (self-)care. Yet, a pertinent question is whether certain care relations are contingent on digital dependencies between people and, despite being perceived as burdensome, should therefore not be broken through disconnection. Drawing on feminist ethics of care, which understands care as all the work that maintains everyday life, this article examines how care and digital dis/connection practices shape each other. Empirically, it draws on ethnographic fieldwork with 20 adults and analyses three vignettes through a relational framework that follows care occurring in, through and away from digital devices. The findings show that digital well-being is shaped less by individual media use than by the care relations that digital technologies sustain. Experiences of digital dis/connection reveal how connectivity is embedded in often invisible responsibilities, dependencies, and forms of care. Rather than locating digital tensions in technologies themselves, the analysis suggests that such tensions expose underlying challenges in how care is organised, valued, and distributed. In response, the article develops the framework of careful dis/connection to evaluate digital practices according to how they sustain, redistribute, and make visible the care on which everyday life depends.

item.title: Press freedom in a post-authoritarian context: evolving challenges for Bangladeshi journalists after Sheikh Hasina
item.dc:creator: Manwar Hossain, Mahbubul Haque Bhuiyan, Muhammad Saurav Rahman, Md Saddam Hossain
item.description:
Journalism · Manwar Hossain, Mahbubul Haque Bhuiyan, Muhammad Saurav Rahman, Md Saddam Hossain

Topics: Press freedom, Journalism, Political communication, Journalistic practice

Authoritarian constraints on press freedom manifest across diverse political contexts, from typical illiberal democracies to flawed democracies. While substantial scholarship examines journalistic challenges under authoritarian rule, the dynamics of press freedom in recent post-authoritarian transitions remain underexplored. Drawing on in-depth interviews with journalists from Bangladesh, this article investigates how press freedom evolves in these settings. Findings show that an authoritarian regime change does not guarantee press freedom or journalist safety. The study makes three theoretical contributions. First, ownership structures and political pressures from authoritarian periods persist after regime transitions. Second, control over the press may shift from predictable, top-down tools (laws and state agencies) to more scattered, bottom-up forces, such as street intimidation and social media harassment. Finally, the press-power relationship is often renegotiated rather than automatically liberalized following authoritarian collapse.

item.dc:creator: Zoya Ivanova
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Zoya Ivanova

item.title: The role of democratic values in shaping perceptions of political incivility in European liberal democracies
item.dc:creator: Sara Bentivegna, Rossella Rega
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Sara Bentivegna, Rossella Rega

Topics: Political incivility, Democratic values, Political polarization, Cross-cultural communication

This study investigates whether citizens’ perceptions of political incivility converge across liberal democracies and the extent to which individual orientations towards democracy and democratic values are associated with sensitivity to incivility. Drawing on a comparative survey conducted in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom ( N = 3500), it examines the individual factors associated with sensitivity to incivility. The results show that support for democracy and endorsement of democratic values are the most influential predictors of sensitivity to incivility, with higher levels associated with greater sensitivity, whereas anti-political attitudes are associated with lower sensitivity. These findings indicate that sensitivity to incivility is primarily associated with citizens’ orientations towards democracy and its normative principles rather than with national contextual differences. Citizens in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom assess incivility in remarkably similar ways, despite differences in electoral systems, media systems, and political cultures.

item.title: From Hate Speech to Collective Action Intentions: The Role of Counter-Speech and Accuracy Cues Among Targeted Minorities
item.dc:creator: Desirée Schmuck, Magdalena Obermaier, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Muniba Saleem
item.description:
Communication Research · Desirée Schmuck, Magdalena Obermaier, Nancy Molina-Rogers, Muniba Saleem

Topics: Online hate speech, Counter-speech, Collective action, Social identity

Online hate speech targeting minority groups poses a significant social identity threat to those affected, often prompting coping strategies like out-group avoidance or derogation, which can harm intergroup relations in diverse societies. However, collective action as an empowering response has received limited attention in this context. Drawing on the social identity model of collective action (SIMCA), this study examines both the mechanisms and boundary conditions of online hate speech’s impact on minority groups. Across two experiments ( N Study1 = 328 Muslims; N Study2 = 583 Latinos), we find that online hate speech increases group-based injustice, which in turn drives collective action intentions, supporting the SIMCA. This effect is amplified when information embedded in the online hate speech is perceived as inaccurate or flagged for inaccuracy. In Study 2, we further demonstrate that counter-speech can reduce group-based injustice and, when paired with low-accuracy hate speech, enhance collective efficacy beliefs.
