item.title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress
item.dc:creator: Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Oori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Oori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Mental health, Generative AI, Attachment orientation

General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

item.title: Internet Addiction Disorder and Cybersecurity Risk: A Neurobiological and Behavioral Review
item.dc:creator: Daniel Robinson, Ray Robinson
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Daniel Robinson, Ray Robinson

Topics: Internet addiction, Well-being, Digital well-being, Social engineering

Internet addiction disorder (IAD) has attracted substantial clinical and scientific interest over the past two decades. Although the condition remains outside formal diagnostic frameworks in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, accumulating neuroimaging evidence demonstrates that compulsive Internet use is associated with disruptions in dopaminergic reward circuitry and prefrontal cortical function that closely parallel those observed in substance use disorders. These neurobiological changes, encompassing impaired executive function, elevated impulsivity, and heightened reward sensitivity, may carry implications for cybersecurity. Available evidence suggests that individuals exhibiting addictive patterns of Internet use show reduced compliance with security protocols, increased vulnerability to social engineering, and elevated engagement in risky online behaviors, although directionality cannot be established with confidence given the predominantly cross-sectional evidence base. The present narrative review synthesizes evidence from addiction neuroscience, clinical psychology, and cybersecurity research to propose a mechanistic account of the IAD-cybersecurity risk relationship. The review identifies impaired prefrontal inhibitory control as the central neurobiological mediator linking IAD to cybersecurity vulnerability, mediated primarily through impulsivity and compounded by the attentional and affective characteristics that render addicted individuals susceptible to social engineering. Drawing on literature spanning 2017-2026, the review also situates this account within a contemporary regulatory context, including the documented acceleration of problematic Internet use during the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia's landmark social media minimum age legislation, and an influential 2026 civil verdict in which a U.S. jury found major platform operators liable for harms arising from addictive design. Clinical, organizational, and policy implications are discussed.

item.title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
item.dc:creator: Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim

Topics: Media addiction, Parent-child play, Executive function, Longitudinal study

Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent-child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent-child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent-child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent-child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.

item.title: The perturbing voice: Minority journalists and the struggle for journalistic legitimacy in Thailand’s Deep South
item.dc:creator: Treepon Kirdnark
item.description:
Journalism · Treepon Kirdnark

Topics: Journalistic legitimacy, Journalism, Social media, Political communication

While scholarly attention to journalistic legitimacy is growing, most studies remain concentrated in the West, overlooking the experiences of journalists in the Global South. To redress this gap, this study draws on in-depth interviews with five Muslim minority journalists in Thailand’s Deep South who actively counter Thai state narratives through social media. It examines how these journalists perform boundary work to establish legitimacy while operating amid armed conflict, securitization, and intense state surveillance. The findings identify three emerging practices that enable these minority journalists to claim the role of “partisan truth-teller”. First, they employ social media to assert cultural authority as “partisan narrators” sharing close proximity to local communities marginalized by the Thai state. Second, they use such platforms to challenge the “views” of outsiders and resist the Thai public’s widespread distrust of Malay Muslims. Finally, they confront security authorities, thereby reclaiming citizen rights and advocating for the security of Malay Muslims. In contrast to Western models of journalism as “public service”, this study contends that legitimacy in this context derives mainly from the enactment of “truth” via “partisan and perturbing voices” that defend the rights of Malay Muslim communities in Thailand.

item.title: Media Use for Strong and Weak Ties: A Configural Examination of Personal Media System and Well-Being
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Zhang, Ronald E. Rice
item.description:
Communication Research · Xinyi Zhang, Ronald E. Rice

Topics: Well-being, Digital stress, Social networks, Media use

Taking a configural approach to personal media use, this study examined how strong- and weak-tie media configuration relate to digital stress and well-being. Using a sample of 1,197 U.S. adults (analytic N = 1,143), we explored how media configuration attributes (size, density, and centralization by tie strength, and homogeneity) are associated with well-being, directly and indirectly through five dimensions of digital stress (overconnectivity, communication overload, deficient self-regulation, self-presentation pressure, and technological frustration). Our results highlight the importance of maintaining a larger, more interconnected, and centralized weak-tie configuration, and overall, a more uniform configuration, for well-being benefits (direct and indirect). Notably, larger weak-tie configuration is indirectly associated with lower well-being through greater technological frustration, while larger strong-tie configuration is indirectly associated with higher well-being through lower technological frustration. These findings emphasize the relational context of communication media use and suggest tie-specific strategies for managing communication flows and supporting well-being.

item.title: Stratified Mobile Parenting Capital: Restrictive, Reformist and Radical Parenting Among Rural Migrant Working Families in China
item.dc:creator: Na Liu, Yutian Xiong
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Na Liu, Yutian Xiong

Topics: Mobile parenting capital, Digital inequality, Digital divide, Digital media

This study proposes the concept of mobile parenting capital, defined as the knowledge and capacities that parents draw upon to mobilise resources across spaces to support their parenting. Through interviews and observations with rural migrant worker parents, social workers and teachers in China, the study identifies three stratified parenting strategies: restrictive, reformist and radical. Restrictive parents possess limited digital resources and rely heavily on rural schools. Reformist parents actively employ digital tools to facilitate translocal parenting and support their left-behind children. Radical parents, who frequently relocate their children between rural hometowns and urban destinations, accumulate the highest levels of mobile parenting capital, while further mobilising resources from both urban and rural contexts digitally and physically.

item.title: Digital Agency Tools: A Way to Buffer the Negative Effects of Excessive Phone Use?
item.dc:creator: Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay

Topics: Smartphone use, Digital well-being, Well-being, Mobile media

In times of ubiquitous smartphone use, most users adopt one or more self-imposed rules regarding their device usage, also known as voluntary digital disconnection. Drawing on the Integrative Model of Mobile Media Use and Need Experiences (IM³UNE), this study provides empirical evidence on the adoption of digital agency tools and their potential in mitigating ill-being (depression, anxiety, and stress) associated with excessive smartphone use. We conducted a quota-based online survey involving n = 384 ( M age = 49.6) smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium). The results provide a systematization of different digital agency tools, showing they are widely used among adults. Importantly, we provide preliminary evidence on their potential in buffering ill-being due to excessive smartphone use. For users of detox apps and in-app well-being features, the associations between excessive use and ill-being were nonsignificant, unlike for nonusers of these tools. For users of default device settings, such as iOS ScreenTime, there were no differences. Our findings contribute to theory by applying and empirically testing critical elements of the IM³UNE model. Empirically, our findings indicate the importance of studying different types of tools, as they do not appear to be equally beneficial.

item.title: War or humanitarian crisis? A framing analysis of flemish media coverage of Gaza in 2023 and 2024
item.dc:creator: Gianni Blok, Ans De Nolf
item.description:
Journalism · Gianni Blok, Ans De Nolf

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Journalism, Political communication

This study analyzes how the Gaza conflict is framed in Flemish media, focusing on articles from De Standaard (DS) and Het Laatste Nieuws (HLN). Coverage was examined during three key moments over 1 year: the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, the bombings of Rafah starting May 6, 2024, and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant on November 21, 2024. Using an existing framing matrix, the study investigated (1) which frames were used, (2) how they differed between newspapers, and (3) whether they shifted across time. The results show that the human interest frame, followed by the war frame, dominated coverage in both newspapers. In the first two periods, the three most common frames were similar across DS and HLN. Only in the third period (November 2024) did the most frequently used frames differ. Over time, different framings emerged for each event, although human interest and war frames remained consistently present. Both outlets relied primarily on Western sources, leading to a potential source bias. Compared to DS, HLN presented events in a less nuanced way, which is expected from a popular newspaper. This study offers new insight into Flemish media representations of the Gaza conflict, a largely underexplored subject.

item.title: Du Boisian practice & thought for journalism studies
item.dc:creator: Tyler Leeds
item.description:
Journalism · Tyler Leeds

Topics: Journalism studies, Black press, Journalistic practice, Journalism history

W.E.B. Du Bois was a massively important 20th century journalist and intellectual. However, his journalistic practice and social theorizing are not often retrieved by journalism studies scholars as analytic resources. To make the case for his utility, I first demonstrate how Du Bois alters scholarly analyses of the 1619 Project that stress the effort’s novelty. In contrast, I situate the 1619 Project in a Du Boisian tradition marked by empiricism and positive propaganda, a combination which swims against professional journalists’ emic understandings of objectivity. I then tour moments of Du Bois’s career that show how he theorized processes of interest to journalism scholars, including his analysis of the Black press and his wider theorizing of discursive culture and its impact on habitual racism. I conclude by contrasting Du Bois to his contemporary and correspondent Walter Lippmann.

item.title: From normative principles to epistemic governance: A workflow-based analysis of European journalism ethics in datafied environments
item.dc:creator: Laurence Dierickx, Marília Gehrke, Carl‐Gustav Lindén
item.description:
Journalism · Laurence Dierickx, Marília Gehrke, Carl‐Gustav Lindén

Topics: Data journalism, Journalism ethics, Datafication, Automated journalism

Data journalism has received limited attention in journalism ethics, where it is often assumed that established normative principles apply directly to data-driven practices. However, data journalism relies on complex data processes that introduce distinct epistemic challenges related to bias, interpretation, and accountability. This study examines data journalism ethics as a form of epistemic governance embedded across key stages of the data journalism workflow, from data gathering to data visualisation, drawing on a thematic analysis of 37 ethical codes from 32 European countries. The findings show that, while ethical codes consistently articulate principles such as accuracy, fairness, and transparency, they rarely operationalise them in relation to methodological decisions shaping data-driven reporting. The epistemic governance framework serves as a bridge between data journalism ethics and AI ethics, as many AI-related ethical challenges originate in data practices and are intensified by automation.

item.title: Responsibility vs. sensationalism: A cross-cultural review of media coverage of sexual violence
item.dc:creator: Mian Ahmad Hanan, Noshina Saleem, Nasim Ishaq, Masroor Ahmed, Arooj Arshad, Imran Saeed
item.description:
Journalism · Mian Ahmad Hanan, Noshina Saleem, Nasim Ishaq, Masroor Ahmed, Arooj Arshad, Imran Saeed

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Cross-cultural communication, Media effects

In this study, the media coverage of various incidents of sexual violence across the various countries of the world has been analyzed, and to surface that whether the media is responsible, sensational or neutral in coverage of such events. Media Coverage of sexual violence is examined in the context of Galdi and Guizzo (2021), the Media-Induced Sexual Harassment (MISH) framework and Simon and Gagnon (2003) Sexual Script Theory. The review suggests that sensationalized framing and sexually objectifying representations may reinforce harmful stereotypes, reduce empathy toward survivors, and contribute to public attitudes associated with sexual violence. Through a systematic search, the data was collected from major databases from 2012 to 2021 across major academic and open-access databases, including Google Scholar, PubMed, JSTOR, Web of Science, Sage Journals, and Library Genesis. Out of an initial pool of 172 potentially relevant research articles, the researchers identified and selected 135 articles that were most directly related to their specific research topic sexual violence against women for an in-depth, systematic review. The review indicates that sensational reporting remains more prevalent than responsible reporting across many cultural contexts, although important regional differences were identified.

item.title: Ten years of the mobile world congress: Media impact on the city of Barcelona
item.dc:creator: Marta Gil Ibáñez, Silvia Guillén Ruiz, Lara Martín-Vicario, Javier Bustos Díaz
item.description:
Journalism · Marta Gil Ibáñez, Silvia Guillén Ruiz, Lara Martín-Vicario, Javier Bustos Díaz

Topics: Media coverage, Sentiment analysis, Journalism, City branding

The Mobile World Congress (MWC) has become an international benchmark in mobile technology and one of the most significant events hosted in Barcelona. Beyond its technological relevance, its media visibility may have played a key role in shaping the city’s public image and international reputation. This study aims to examine the impact of media coverage of the Mobile World Congress on the promotion and positioning of the city of Barcelona. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining content analysis and sentiment analysis through the implementation of a hierarchical multiclass automatic classification system. The study analysed news coverage published in three major regional newspapers— La Vanguardia , Ara.Cat , and El Periódico ( n = 3523 news articles). This methodological design enabled the identification of thematic patterns, dominant narratives, and the frequency with which Barcelona was associated with the event. The findings indicate that media coverage of the MWC has had a notably positive effect on Barcelona’s visibility and reputation. The newspapers consistently presented the city as a leading hub for technological innovation, international business, and large-scale global events. Recurrent references to Barcelona’s organisational capacity and strategic relevance within the mobile technology sector contributed to strengthening its urban brand and enhancing its symbolic capital in both regional and international media discourse. The MWC has significantly contributed to boosting and promoting the city of Barcelona. Media representation of the event has reinforced the city’s status as a global, innovation-driven urban centre and has consolidated its position within the international technological landscape.

item.title: Predicting Irritation Disclosures in Romantic Relationships: Testing and Extending the Revelation Risk Model
item.dc:creator: Rudy C. Pett, Anita L. Vangelisti
item.description:
Communication Research · Rudy C. Pett, Anita L. Vangelisti

Topics: Self-disclosure, Interpersonal communication, Relationship power, Longitudinal study

Feelings of irritation often emerge in romantic relationships. However, the theoretical mechanisms predicting whether individuals disclose these feelings to their romantic partner remain limited and largely reliant on examining indicators of future behavior rather than actual future behavior. Using a two-month, longitudinal survey design involving 448 participants, the current study tested the Revelation Risk Model (RRM) as a mechanism for predicting whether individuals would disclose or conceal feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power was also incorporated as an additional predictor. The original RRM components (i.e., closeness, risk, communication efficacy, willingness to disclose) collectively predicted whether individuals disclosed or concealed feelings of irritation about their romantic partner. Relationship power predicted individuals’ communication efficacy, as well as perceived risk associated with disclosing their feelings of irritation. The findings are discussed in terms of their contributions to existing research on disclosure, irritations, and power in romantic relationships.

item.title: mlstats : An R Package for Multilevel Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation
item.dc:creator: Felix Dietrich
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Felix Dietrich

Topics: Research methodology, Computational methods, Measurement validity, Mobile communication

Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats , an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics—including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations—in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on Comprehensive R Archive Network with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/ .

item.title: LENS—LLM Effects on News Scrutiny: Influence, Delegation, and Memory in AI-Mediated News
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Reina, Stefania La Rocca, Federico Longoni, Giuseppe Riva
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Lorenzo Reina, Stefania La Rocca, Federico Longoni, Giuseppe Riva

Topics: Large Language Models, Generative AI, News consumption, Artificial intelligence in journalism

item.title: Weekly Gaming Duration and Internet Gaming Disorder in Relation to Depression and Loneliness: A Two-Year Follow-Up Study
item.dc:creator: Joshua J. Condry, Isabel C. Singer, Zachary A. Reese
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Joshua J. Condry, Isabel C. Singer, Zachary A. Reese

Topics: Video games, Internet Gaming Disorder, Depression, Loneliness

The current study examined the association between weekly video game engagement and mental health, specifically Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD), loneliness, and depression. We recruited 377 U.S. adults through CloudResearch Connect using gaming-frequency quotas, resulting in a sample representing a wide range of weekly gaming duration (range = 0–80 hours, M = 14.62). Analyses revealed that weekly gameplay hours did not consistently predict depression and loneliness. In contrast, people with higher IGD scores tended to have higher weekly playtime, more depressive symptoms, and greater feelings of loneliness. We readministered the same survey 2 years later ( N = 172 or 45.6 percent of baseline sample). Here, we found that both higher weekly hours and higher IGD scores at baseline predicted increases in depressive symptoms 2 years later, controlling for their baseline depression. We did not find that gaming was predictive of loneliness longitudinally. These findings are particularly relevant given the American Psychiatric Association’s interest in IGD in the DSM-5 coupled with the ongoing public debate about the benefits and ills of video games. Our findings suggest that people who struggle to balance gaming with other life demands may experience more depressive symptoms over time. Thus, clinicians may opt to focus on helping clients with IGD better balance their priorities.

item.title: Feeling the crisis, building the alternative: Women journalists in nonprofit digital media through the lens of feminist epistemology and the affective turn
item.dc:creator: Majda Hrženjak
item.description:
Journalism · Majda Hrženjak

Topics: Journalism, Alternative media, Feminist epistemology, Digital media

This article draws on feminist standpoint epistemology and the affective turn to examine how women journalists respond to deteriorating working conditions in Slovenian legacy media. The study focuses on three analytically selected cases of women journalists who co-founded nonprofit, women-led digital media outlets, drawn from 15 exploratory autobiographical interviews. Their narratives articulate experiences of marginalization alongside agentic responses that critically interrogate developments in the legacy media system and call for a rethinking of journalistic ethics and labor organization. Journalism is approached as affective labor, marked by the entanglement of passion, self-exploitation, and precarity, in which emotions such as anger, care, and responsibility – combined with digital affordances – enable the creation of alternative media spaces. These initiatives are interpreted not merely as individual survival strategies but as micropolitical and epistemological interventions that reclaim professional autonomy and integrity. While embedded in neoliberal conditions and structurally fragile, they demonstrate the potential of alternative practices to reimagine journalism from the margins.

item.title: Explaining Science Knowledge Gaps on Social Media: Basic Science Knowledge and Intentional Versus Incidental Exposure
item.dc:creator: Wenbo Li, Christine Gilbert, Shan Xu
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Wenbo Li, Christine Gilbert, Shan Xu

Topics: Science communication, Social media use, Media literacy, Climate change communication

This study examined whether basic science knowledge helps explain education-based gaps in domain-specific science knowledge and whether intentional and incidental exposure on social media condition those gaps. A national survey of American adults focused on two domains: climate change and algorithms. Results showed that basic science knowledge mediated the relationship between education and domain-specific knowledge across both domains. These indirect relationship were attenuated at higher levels of intentional social media exposure. The findings suggest that strengthening foundational science literacy and encouraging more deliberate engagement with science content on social media may help reduce knowledge disparities.

item.title: Democratic Media Performance and Democratization: A Global Longitudinal Perspective
item.dc:creator: Florian Arendt
item.description:
Communication Research · Florian Arendt

Topics: Democratic media performance, Democratization, Media systems, Political communication

Media that effectively perform their democratic functions are widely considered a key driver of democratization, yet longitudinal evidence on their impact remains limited. This study analyzed global annual time-series data on democratic media performance and democratization from 1946 to 2018. ARIMA models indicated a covariation between annual increases in democratic media performance and gains in democratization worldwide, measured by Vanhanen’s Index of Democratization. The analysis also revealed covariation with V-Dem’s liberal, participatory, deliberative, and egalitarian component indices of democratic quality. Evidence on temporal ordering, consistent with Granger causality, was found for Vanhanen’s index and the participatory and deliberative V-Dem component indices; evidence was marginal for the liberal component and absent for the egalitarian component. Acknowledging limitations regarding causal interpretation, the results are consistent with the claim that media can act as a leading force in democratic development rather than merely reflecting it, particularly in electoral, participatory, and deliberative dimensions.

item.title: Affective journalism and identity: Community newspapers as emotional agents in Hong Kong
item.dc:creator: Han Xiao-ying, Zhi‐Jin Zhong
item.description:
Journalism · Han Xiao-ying, Zhi‐Jin Zhong

Topics: Journalism, Epistemology, Discourse analysis, Political polarization

Situated within Hong Kong’s rapidly shifting sociopolitical context and complex identity landscape, this article examines how community newspapers produce community imaginaries in Hong Kong, focusing on the affective-discursive strategies through which grassroots journalism constructs community knowledge. Treating emotion as an epistemic infrastructure, this article draws on affective epistemology to examine how such strategies in two ideologically divergent community newspapers constitute distinct forms of community knowledge for readers. Through a comparative critical discourse analysis of one pro-democracy and one pro-establishment community newspaper, the analysis identifies two distinct affective strategies: an affective-participatory strategy that constitutes community as a self-determining collective subject, and an affective-governance strategy that constitutes community as a condition of harmony sustained through virtuous individuals and aligned institutions.

item.title: Work-Related Harassment and Intimidation in Journalism: Testing Identity-, Visibility-, and Influence-Based Explanations
item.dc:creator: Ilmari Hiltunen, Ilari Törönen, Aleksi Suuronen, Reeta Pöyhtäri
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Ilmari Hiltunen, Ilari Törönen, Aleksi Suuronen, Reeta Pöyhtäri

Topics: Journalism, Online harassment, Journalistic practice, Press freedom

Prior research shows that exposure to occupation-related harassment and intimidation varies considerably across journalists. This study tests three explanatory frameworks for this variation: identity-based explanations attributing heightened exposure to social hierarchies; visibility- and celebrity-capital-based explanations linking it to journalists’ varying levels of personal visibility and recognizability; and influence-based explanations attributing differences to the nature of journalistic work and its societal influence. Logistic regression analyses of survey data from Finnish journalists ( n = 932), examining verbal, legal, and physical forms of harassment and intimidation, lend strong support to influence-based explanations, partial support to visibility-based explanations, and limited support to identity-based explanations.

item.title: From Algorithms to Affection: Unpacking the Psychological Mechanism of Emotional Attachment Toward Virtual Influencers
item.dc:creator: Hyun Jung Oh, Mikyoung Kim
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Hyun Jung Oh, Mikyoung Kim

Topics: Parasocial relationships, Virtual influencers, Social media influencers, Self-disclosure

As virtual human influencers (VHIs) increasingly inhabit social media landscapes, they are functioning not merely as marketing tools but as social entities capable of eliciting user affection. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying emotional attachment to these artificial agents remain underexplored compared to their human counterparts. This study investigates how VHI self-disclosure influences emotional attachment, positing parasocial relationships as a mediator and perceived attractiveness and humanness as boundary conditions. We analyzed online survey data from 540 young adults familiar with VHIs using a moderated mediation framework. The findings reveal a complex dynamic distinct from human interaction: VHI self-disclosure generally hindered parasocial relationship formation unless the VHI was perceived as physically attractive. This suggests attractiveness acts as a requisite gateway for users to accept artificial disclosure as relationally meaningful. Subsequently, parasocial relationships strongly predicted emotional attachment, an effect significantly amplified by perceived humanness. Consequently, self-disclosure indirectly promoted emotional attachment only when the VHI was viewed as both attractive and human-like. These results delineate the distinct roles of VHI attributes: Attractiveness facilitates the initial establishment of a social connection (parasocial relationship), whereas perceived humanness deepens this bond into a meaningful emotional attachment. Theoretically, this study expands the understanding of human-agent interaction by identifying these differential pathways. Practically, it suggests that developers must prioritize high visual attractiveness to make VHI interactions acceptable, while simultaneously imbuing agents with human-like qualities to foster lasting emotional loyalty.

item.title: The Real-World Effects of Constructive Journalism: A Field Experiment on Climate Change News
item.dc:creator: Morten Skovsgaard
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Morten Skovsgaard

Topics: Journalism, Climate change communication, News coverage, Media effects

To explore the effects of constructive journalism beyond one-shot experiments, this study utilizes a 2-week constructive journalism campaign on climate change in two regional Danish news outlets. Employing a difference-in-differences approach, news users exposed to the campaign were compared to news users from regions not exposed to the campaign. The constructive journalism campaign yielded more positive evaluations of news coverage, but not on core quality aspects like trustworthiness and balance. No effects were found for emotional responses, response efficacy, and behavioural intentions, but a positive effect was found for self-efficacy, indicating the potential of a constructive approach to journalism.

item.title: When Past Hurt Meets Present Care: How Family History Shapes Adult Caregivers’ Communal Coping With Siblings in Their Caregiving for Parents With Health Challenges
item.dc:creator: Abdullah S. Salehuddin, Andy J. Merolla, Tamara D. Afifi
item.description:
Communication Research · Abdullah S. Salehuddin, Andy J. Merolla, Tamara D. Afifi

Topics: Communal coping, Caregiver burden, Family communication, Interpersonal communication

This sequential, explanatory mixed-methods study explores how adult caregivers’ perceived family functioning and unresolved hurt toward siblings from childhood are associated with their present-day communal coping (CC) with their siblings and caregiving outcomes. Study 1 tested a hypothesized moderated mediation model using survey data ( N = 776). The results indicate greater childhood family functioning (consistent with hypotheses) and unresolved hurt (counter to hypotheses) were associated with more CC with siblings. CC, in turn, was associated with less flourishing and greater caregiver burden and sibling resentment. Considering the unexpected positive association between unresolved hurt and CC, Study 2 involved semi-structured interviews with adult caregivers ( N = 30) about their experiences enacting CC with siblings despite residual hurt. The findings suggest unresolved childhood hurt toward siblings often stem from challenging experiences, including neglect and abuse. In addition to impeding sibling CC, unresolved hurt can also complicate efforts toward CC (or render them dysfunctional). This study underscores how childhood experiences have an enduring effect on CC with siblings decades later, especially if past family issues are left unresolved.

item.title: When journalists and scientists sit down to talk: Juggling audience expectations in interactional science podcasts during the COVID-19 pandemic
item.dc:creator: Anna-Lena Oltersdorf
item.description:
Journalism · Anna-Lena Oltersdorf

Topics: Science journalism, Science communication, Podcasts, COVID-19 pandemic

Given the growing relevance of podcasts in science communication, especially science journalism, this paper analyzes interactional science podcasts from a dramaturgical perspective. Scientists and journalists face conflicting expectations from different audiences, ranging from professional peers to a ‘general audience.’ Nevertheless, their interactions tend to be relatively harmonious. This paper addresses this puzzle and asks how journalists and scientists juggle audience expectations in different roles. It is based on a qualitative analysis of 15 episodes of the prominent German podcast ‘Coronavirus Update,’ sampled through mentions in metajournalistic discourse during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany. The analysis shows that conflicting expectations require a certain variation within role constellations: actors speak as (co-)moderator, (co-)expert, and as a representative of the audience. The constellations are stabilized through mutual support of each other’s self-presentation, but also the intentional withdrawal thereof in risky situations. Unpacking those interactional dynamics, shaped by audience expectations, helps to understand the social dimension of science journalism and its emerging practices, such as podcasting.

item.title: Smartphone-Based GenAI and the Ruralization of Indian-Language News
item.dc:creator: Subin Paul
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Subin Paul

Topics: Generative AI, Journalism, Digital media, Mobile media

This paper investigates the impact of smartphone-based generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the editing and increasing representation of rural news in Hindi-language speed news in India. As an innovation, speed news refers to the recitation of news summaries by presenters at an accelerated pace across mobile, television, and digital platforms such as YouTube. Drawing on the anthropological conception of “ruralization” and fieldwork in northern India, I argue that smartphone-based GenAI enables small, rural actors working mainly with mobile phones to more effectively condense and edit speed news stories. Smartphone-based GenAI tools such as ChatGPT help package raw speed news stories into pithy, punchy sentences that resemble a form of kahawat (“saying”) or sutra (“aphorism”), thereby striking cultural chords with Hindi-language news audiences, particularly in rural India. This improved news-editing process also facilitates the steady production of speed news bulletins, contributing to the deeper ruralization of Hindi news. The commentary concludes with a brief reflection on the potentials and pitfalls of smartphone-based GenAI in India.

item.title: Building Deep Data Through Screens: Princeton-SMART for Mobile Communication Research
item.dc:creator: Jihye Lee, Kentaro Oriuchi, Daniel Muise, Jacob N. Shapiro
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Jihye Lee, Kentaro Oriuchi, Daniel Muise, Jacob N. Shapiro

Topics: Mobile communication, Digital trace data, Mobile media, Computational methods

This article introduces Princeton-SMART, open-source screen-capture software designed to generate deep data on mobile communication behavior. Princeton-SMART unobtrusively collects screenshots and on-screen text from Android devices at short intervals in naturalistic settings. We describe a research pipeline for secure data collection, preprocessing, and analysis, drawing on over 1.5 million screenshots contributed by U.S. job seekers over 6 weeks. We demonstrate how job-search activities can be identified using vision-language AI models and methodological considerations encountered during the process. We conclude by discussing opportunities and practical implications for integrating Princeton-SMART into mobile communication research.

item.title: Institutional realism in media culture: How disability journalism education reveals structural limits of cultural change
item.dc:creator: Faith Valencia‐Forrester
item.description:
Journalism · Faith Valencia‐Forrester

Topics: Journalism education, Journalistic practice, Professional norms, Media representation

Media institutions systematically exclude disability perspectives despite decades of advocacy and educational intervention. This article examines why cultural transformation efforts fail to penetrate professional media practice, extending Mark Fisher’s concept of ‘capitalist realism’ to reveal how institutional realism operates: we can imagine transformed practitioners but not transformed institutions. Drawing on critical autoethnographic analysis of two contrasting disability reporting education initiatives, an intensive community-partnered program and widely-distributed industry guidance, I demonstrate how professional socialisation functions as a mechanism of cultural reproduction, systematically neutralising educational gains through reification processes. While both interventions demonstrably transformed individual practitioners, neither disrupted what Jacques Rancière (2004) terms the ‘distribution of the sensible’ that determines whose voices become audible in media discourse. This case contributes to critical theory by specifying how institutional realism lets institutions appear to embrace cultural change while containing it. The analysis reveals a depth-versus-scale paradox: interventions intensive enough to transform how practitioners see disability cannot be scaled, while interventions that scale reach only those already disposed to change. It specifies two frameworks: the distinction between epistemic transformation and behavioural modification, and the mechanism through which newsroom routines reify ableist assumptions as professional competence, and positional disability expertise as optional specialisation rather than core.

item.title: The meaning and viability of redress: How newspapers and polls frame reparations
item.dc:creator: Sean P. Pauley
item.description:
Journalism · Sean P. Pauley

Topics: Media framing, News framing, Public opinion, Political polarization

Despite reparations for slavery being part of the historical struggle for racial justice in the United States, the issue has fallen at the periphery of political discourse. Yet, in 2019 and 2020, the news devoted substantially more attention to the issue as Democratic primary candidates discussed it in debates and it was championed by the Movement for Black Lives. However, despite the fact we know that coverage increased during this time, we know surprisingly little about how reparations were discussed. This study analyzes the framing decisions present in opinion pieces across three of the largest U.S. national newspapers—and how these decisions interacted with public opinion polling and general election coverage in 2019 and 2020. I find that reparations were commonly discussed without mentioning any specific form. Instead, the issue framed as one of many radical and unpopular issues championed by people on the far left before the 2020 election.

item.title: The polarized talk least about polarization: Polarization discourses in tabloids and broadsheets from UK, Germany and Sweden
item.dc:creator: Mike Farjam, Hendrik Meyer, Anamaria Dutceac Segesten, Michael Brüggemann
item.description:
Journalism · Mike Farjam, Hendrik Meyer, Anamaria Dutceac Segesten, Michael Brüggemann

Topics: Political polarization, News coverage, Media framing, Journalism

This study examines how newspapers from three distinct national contexts—the UK, Germany, and Sweden—report about polarization, and how such coverage makes societal division visible and emotionally salient. Drawing on 230,000 news articles from 2014 to 2023, we use Word2Vec, Named Entity Recognition, topic modeling, and anger classification to identify and analyze journalistic metadiscourse about polarization and broader division. Across countries and outlets, references to polarization increased markedly during the decade. Sweden, the least polarized country in our comparison, showed the highest volume of polarization discourse. Tabloids generally feature higher levels of anger in broader coverage but report less often about polarization than broadsheets. These findings are consistent with a reflexive-journalism logic, whereby polarization discourse is most frequent in outlets that interpret and contextualize broader societal developments, rather than in the most polarized settings. The study highlights the need for cross-national perspectives on how media frame and write about societal division.

item.title: Economic Conditions, Public Sentiment, and News Coverage: A Time-Series Analysis of Economic Agenda Dynamics in South Korea
item.dc:creator: Sei-Hill Kim, Wansoo Lee
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Sei-Hill Kim, Wansoo Lee

Topics: Agenda-setting, News coverage, Public opinion, Journalism

Drawing on 23 years of economic news in South Korea, this study investigates how key economic indicators interact with the volume and tone of economic news, which can both shape and reflect public opinion, particularly the public’s economic sentiment. Time-series analyses revealed that unfavorable economic conditions, reflected in lower Stock Market Index and GDP growth rates as well as higher Consumer Price Index (CPI) and unemployment rates, were associated with greater news coverage of these topics in the subsequent month. The tone of news coverage was largely unrelated to economic indicators, suggesting that the overall news sentiment may not closely align with real-world economic conditions. Finally, the relationship between economic news and public sentiment was reciprocal rather than one-directional. Implications for economic journalism are discussed in detail.

item.title: “ In a way, I want TikTok to tell me what I want. . . ” Users’ experience of TikTok as a televisual algorithmic flow
item.dc:creator: Carlos Entrena-Serrano, Trisha Meyer, Emília Gómez, Jos Pierson
item.description:
New Media & Society · Carlos Entrena-Serrano, Trisha Meyer, Emília Gómez, Jos Pierson

Topics: TikTok, Social media algorithms, Small Acts of Engagement, Audience engagement

This article revisits Williams’s concept of flow, Firth’s notion of algorithmic flow, and Picone et al.’s concept of Small Acts of Engagement (SAOE) to examine how users experience TikTok’s algorithmic flow. SAOE are understood as low-effort, everyday acts through which users negotiate their identities and shape their digital consumption. While SAOE have been a valuable lens for understanding user agency on earlier social media platforms, we argue that TikTok’s interface design and cultural framing introduce new challenges. The platform’s design, together with users’ perception of TikTok’s algorithmic flow as a televisual experience, reduces their SAOE to a minimal expression: a rhythm of watch, scroll, repeat , discouraging other forms of intentional, identity-driven engagement. Through a mixed-methods study combining interviews and analysis of participants’ donated TikTok data, we show how our participants experience TikTok as a place for effortless entertainment and continuous consumption, closely resembling the experience of traditional television flow.

item.title: Anchored in capital: A Bourdieusian analysis of journalistic identity and resilience in the Portuguese field
item.dc:creator: Rui Alexandre Novais
item.description:
Journalism · Rui Alexandre Novais

Topics: Journalistic identity, Professional norms, Journalism studies, Digital disruption

This repeated cross-sectional study (2013-2023) examines the resilience of professional values in Portuguese journalism amid economic precarity and digital disruption. Integrating Bourdieu’s field theory with Raemy’s multi-level identity model, we show how journalists reinforce symbolic capital—intensifying watchdog roles and ethical norms—to preserve field autonomy. Using data from two waves of the Worlds of Journalism Study-Portugal, we analyze how this defensive consolidation operates through capital conversion across macro, meso, and micro levels. The findings reframe value stability not as inertia but as active identity work, offering insights into how peripheral media systems sustain professional coherence under duress.

item.title: Prompting with Respect: Cultural Norms and User Experience in LLM Interactions
item.dc:creator: Sujin Yang, Seoyoung Oh, Ha Eun Shim
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Sujin Yang, Seoyoung Oh, Ha Eun Shim

Topics: Generative AI, Large Language Models, Human-AI interaction, Cross-cultural communication

Despite growing interest in prompt engineering, its influence on user experience-particularly in relation to cultural communication norms-remains largely unexplored. This controlled experiment examined how respectful versus directive prompting-a culturally meaningful contrast in Korean-affects Korean users' psychological experience during LLM interactions. Forty-three Korean female college students were randomly assigned to respectful prompt (RP) (using polite requests, compliments, and gratitude) or directive prompt (DP) (using imperatives, criticism, and performance-based penalties) conditions. Participants completed a writing task using ChatGPT. Results indicated that RPs yielded significantly higher satisfaction, particularly for affinity and likability, whereas the difference in perceived output quality was smaller and nonsignificant. Furthermore, RPs elicited socially supportive ChatGPT responses, whereas DPs were followed by apologies, suggesting bidirectional social adaptation between users and ChatGPT. Together, these findings suggest that culturally grounded communicative conventions may shape users' subjective experience even where perceived output quality does not differ significantly, pointing to culturally adaptive large language model systems that recognize diverse communication patterns as essential design considerations rather than imposing universal paradigms.

item.title: Stigma, erasure, and change: Newspaper coverage of prostitution in the mid-20th century
item.dc:creator: Mary Angela Bock, Soojeong Kim, Aruna Muthupillai
item.description:
Journalism · Mary Angela Bock, Soojeong Kim, Aruna Muthupillai

Topics: Gender representation, Journalism studies, News coverage, Content analysis

This project studied news articles about prostitution in the mid-century U.S. to explore the impact of second wave feminism on coverage. Based on a content analysis of 630 articles downloaded from Newspapers.com from the 1950s, ‘60s and ‘70s, it found that while patriarchal values dominated coverage overall, changes could be discerned in the 1970s. Typically, women’s voices were linguistically marginalized even when they were included in coverage. Men, whether as news reporters or as members of law enforcement, were usually the framers of such stories, and when women were included, they were rarely named and quoted far less often. Yet as more women wrote news in the 1970s, stories reflected more concern for women involved in prostitution and were more likely to include their voice. The findings contribute to feminist scholarship and studies of the history of news by underscoring how such coverage, reflected, reinforced, or challenged broader societal hierarchies and power dynamics.

item.title: Greening Mobile AI?
item.dc:creator: Gerard Michael Goggin
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Gerard Michael Goggin

Topics: Mobile media, Artificial intelligence, Digital media, Platform studies

Mobile AI is very much a work in progress. No better time at the outset, then, to consider its environmental implications. As mobile media and communication are woven together with AI, what are their entanglements—and what are the implications for the environment? First, given the slow progress on concerted effort over many years to tackle reuse, repair and ‘greening’ of mobile phones, as well as other mobile technology devices, and associated information and communication technologies, and the research and critique engaging with this endeavour—it is critical to consider the best focus as we move into the AI phone and beyond-the-phone future. Second, the article dissects key trends and issues—hot spots—in the environmental implications of the wider networks, infrastructures, systems and ecologies where mobiles and AI are being deployed in combination—but their ecological implications deserve greater attention. Third, the article proposes priority elements for the research and policy agenda in greening mobile AI.

item.title: “X is simply broken”: The relationship between political journalists and politicians on social media during the 2025 German federal election campaign
item.dc:creator: Matthias Degen, Jonathan Hendrickx
item.description:
Journalism · Matthias Degen, Jonathan Hendrickx

Topics: Political communication, Social media, Political journalism, Election campaigns

Contemporary election campaigns are marked by a move from political parties and politicians to communicating directly to audiences via social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. In doing so, they deliberately bypass journalistic rigour and scrutiny to focus on more personal messages and storytelling techniques. Scholarship has investigated this from the perspective of social media platform logics and political campaigning but has thus far somewhat neglected the journalistic dimension. Using the case study of the snap German federal elections held in February 2025, this contribution features expert interviews with a diverse range of German political journalists and investigates their perspectives on a) how leading politicians used social media platforms in their campaigns and b) how they use said platforms themselves for news sourcing and diffusion as well as direct communication with politicians. Findings reveal a shift away from X (formerly Twitter) and a stronger focus on more outspoken audiovisual platforms such as TikTok for news sourcing and diffusion purposes, while ascribing growing relevance to LinkedIn and even traditional text messages. Politicians’ messages are perceived as steering away from overt political messages, feeding into the ongoing debate about the depoliticization of political communication.

item.title: The power of conversational writing style: Examining the influence of sourcing and writing style on credibility in community journalism
item.dc:creator: Chun Hong Tse, Kecheng Fang
item.description:
Journalism · Chun Hong Tse, Kecheng Fang

Topics: Journalism, News credibility, Citizen journalism, Narrative persuasion

This article revisits the issue of the credibility of citizen journalism in the context of community news. By unpacking its two major reporting characteristics — sourcing from citizens and conversational writing style — this study contributes to our understanding of what makes citizen journalism trustworthy. A 2 (sourcing: elite vs citizen) × 2 (writing style: conversational vs professional) between-subjects experiment ( N = 311) was conducted in Taiwan in late January 2024. Results showed that conversational writing style was considered more credible and more narratively transported than professional journalistic writing. Besides, media skepticism moderated the relationship between conversational writing style and narrative transportation. This implies that, at least concerning community topics, conversational writing style emerges as the critical factor enabling citizen journalism to win trust among the public. Furthermore, results suggest a need to reconsider the rigid professional journalistic norms in certain settings, as the traditional reporting style creates a distance with readers and may be unsuitable for addressing personal-related or emotionally charged topics such as community news and disaster news.

item.title: More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
item.dc:creator: Xucheng Cao, Shuhua Zhou, Jinye Zhu, Xiaohui Wang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Xucheng Cao, Shuhua Zhou, Jinye Zhu, Xiaohui Wang

Topics: Multimodal analysis, Social media engagement, Journalism, Content analysis

This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.

item.title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
item.dc:creator: Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir
item.description:
New Media & Society · Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir

Topics: Online collective action, Social movements, Perceived motives, Social identity

Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.

item.title: Cross-platformization: How U.S. right-leaning media curate their posts on Twitter and Truth Social
item.dc:creator: Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield
item.description:
New Media & Society · Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield

Topics: Social media platforms, Political polarization, Platform affordances, News organizations

This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

item.title: Disappearing Voices, Emerging Resistance: Journalism, Language, and Social Inequality in the U.S.-Mexico Borderlands
item.dc:creator: Jéssica Retis, Susan Barnett, Liliana Lopez Ruelas
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Jéssica Retis, Susan Barnett, Liliana Lopez Ruelas

Topics: Journalism, News deserts, Community engagement, Digital inequality

This article examines how linguistic, geographic, and racial inequalities shape journalism in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Focusing on Southern Arizona, it analyzes the rise of two community-driven Spanish-language news startups following the closure of the city’s only Spanish-language newspaper. Emerging in connection with a bilingual journalism initiative at a local university, these projects developed through collaborative research, community engagement, and newsroom experimentation aimed at addressing gaps in local news coverage. Drawing on research-action practices, collaborative research, and self-ethnography, the study examines how marginalized communities resist exclusion by producing culturally relevant media. It situates these efforts within broader discussions of news deserts, institutional inequality, and the systemic neglect of linguistic minorities, offering insight into how grassroots journalism—and the institutional spaces that can help incubate it—can challenge dominant media norms and reimagine local news in underserved, multilingual communities.

item.title: Being journalists on social media: Contrasting professionals’ self-perceptions to role expectations among adolescents
item.dc:creator: Vasco Avides Moreira, Darian Harff
item.description:
Journalism · Vasco Avides Moreira, Darian Harff

Topics: Journalistic roles, Social media, Journalism, Professional norms

On social media, efforts by individual journalists to share news with audiences may be a viable response to personality-driven news presentation coming from peripheral actors like influencers, who are increasingly popular information sources for adolescents. Yet, when using social media to disseminate content, journalists may risk backlash, especially when innovative approaches represent a deviation from traditional journalistic norms. Drawing on expectancy violations theory and semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted among Portuguese journalists ( N = 7) and adolescents ( N = 20), we contrasted professionals’ own perceptions of being journalists on social media to adolescents’ role expectations. Findings showed that adolescents generally prefer journalists to be personal and independent when presenting news on social media, though they also recognized that journalists may in this context be bound by institutional rules. Similarly, journalists highlighted perceived pressure coming from news organizations and licensing bodies to abide by professional standards, even when using their private social media. Despite seeing value in adopting a ‘newsfluencer’-like role, journalists’ need to negotiate between various interests and expectations represents one of the main hurdles that prevents them from establishing a clear presence on these platforms – and may explain low attraction to journalistic sources on social media among adolescents.

item.title: When even empathy would be enough – Representation of homelessness in the Czech mainstream media during Christmas
item.dc:creator: Vojtěch Dvořák
item.description:
Journalism · Vojtěch Dvořák

Topics: Media representation, News coverage, Media framing, Media coverage

Homelessness remains one of the most persistent and complex societal issues globally, and the media play a significant role in shaping both representations of and public attitudes toward this marginalized population. This study presents a thematic analysis of Czech mainstream news coverage of homelessness during three consecutive Christmas periods (2022, 2023, and 2024). While Christmas coverage might be expected to foreground empathy, humanization, or solidarity more strongly than routine reporting, the analysis shows that such elements remained relatively marginal in the Czech material examined here. The findings reveal a persistent scarcity of solidarity and empathy, with media portrayals frequently reinforcing harmful stereotypes rather than challenging them. The study concludes that substantial changes in media discourse are necessary to promote more accurate and just representations of homelessness in the Czech and possibly further Eastern European context.

item.title: Investigating Conditional Macro-Level Media Effects Over a Long-Term: How Crisis Periods Moderate the Effects of Suicide Coverage on Suicide Rate Change (1861–2007)
item.dc:creator: Christina Viehmann, Stefan Geiß, Manina Mestas, Oliver Quiring, Florian Arendt
item.description:
Communication Research · Christina Viehmann, Stefan Geiß, Manina Mestas, Oliver Quiring, Florian Arendt

Topics: Media effects, Suicide reporting, Long-term media effects, Computational text analysis

How does media shape society over decades, and does its effect vary depending on the societal atmosphere or zeitgeist ? While theoretically important, there is a lack of systematic empirical evidence on conditional long-term macro-level media effects. We propose a broader framework to study such effects and demonstrate its applicability for the “Werther effect” in the UK. More specifically, we investigate whether media coverage of suicides in a newspaper of record is linked to suicide rates and whether this link changes during societal crises. For this, we combine suicide data with a large-scale automated content analysis of crisis and suicide reporting in The Times over a century (1861-2007). Our analysis shows that increased suicide reporting is associated with higher suicide rates, but only during crisis periods. The results are consistent with a conditional Werther effect and may offer one piece of the larger puzzle of long-term macro-level media influences on society.

item.title: Inequality Within the Mobile System: Understanding the Third-Level Digital Divide Through Adverse Digital Incorporation in Rural China
item.dc:creator: Jingke Lin, Jianjie Tao
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Jingke Lin, Jianjie Tao

Topics: Digital divide, Mobile media, Digital inequality, Digital labor

As mobile media rapidly expand in the rural Global South, digital divide research is shifting from an exclusion-based to an inclusion-based perspective. Drawing on Heeks’ “adverse digital incorporation” framework and ethnographic fieldwork in rural China, this article conceptualizes the third-level digital divide, which refers to the unequal outcomes and disparate dividends derived from information and communication technologies, as the unequal extraction of value resulting from power imbalances within the mobile system. The study reveals that this adverse incorporation constitutes two closed loops of value inequality. On the one hand, smartphones break spatiotemporal boundaries to extract value through the commodification of private time, legibility and labor control, and risk-cost shifting. On the other hand, while rural residents employ strategic digital disconnection as a form of everyday resistance, which results in marginalization and reinforces value inequality. Consequently, it is essential to go beyond technical provision to enable rural residents to transform from passive content consumers into active value producers and to rebalance power within the mobile system.

item.title: Relationship Between Cyberbullying and Social Anxiety, School Refusal, and Academic Goals in Adolescents
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Cañas, Mari Carmen Martínez-Monteagudo, Beatriz Delgado, Esther Rubio, David Aparisi
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Elizabeth Cañas, Mari Carmen Martínez-Monteagudo, Beatriz Delgado, Esther Rubio, David Aparisi

Topics: Cyberbullying, Social anxiety, School refusal, Academic goals

Examining the associations between cyberbullying involvement and psychoeducational factors may contribute to a better understanding of adolescents’ experiences in online peer contexts. The aim of this study was to examine the associations between cyberbullying involvement, considering the roles of cybervictim, cyberaggressor, and cyberbystander, and three psychoeducational constructs: social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. A total of 1,412 Spanish secondary and upper-secondary school students aged 12–18 years ( M = 14.36, SD = 1.65) completed a battery of questionnaires assessing cyberbullying, social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. Three independent binary logistic regression models were conducted, one for each cyberbullying role, using the psychoeducational dimensions as predictors. The findings showed that the associations varied according to both the psychoeducational dimension and the cyberbullying role. In particular, Discomfort and avoidance in social situations in general was positively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas other dimensions of social anxiety showed negative associations with some roles. Avoidance of stimuli or situations related to the school context was positively associated with the three cyberbullying roles. Learning and Achievement goals were negatively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas Social reinforcement goals were positively associated with cyberaggression. These findings highlight the multidimensional nature of the associations between psychoeducational factors and cyberbullying involvement and support the consideration of individual and educational variables in the design of prevention and intervention strategies during adolescence.

item.title: Sex, Romance, or Recreation? An Experiment Testing the Effects of Cannabis Brand-generated Social Media Ads on College Students’ Expectancies and Intentions to Use Cannabis Prior to Sex
item.dc:creator: Jessica Fitts Willoughby, Stacey J. T. Hust, Leticia Couto, Jiayu Li, Soojung Kang
item.description:
Communication Research · Jessica Fitts Willoughby, Stacey J. T. Hust, Leticia Couto, Jiayu Li, Soojung Kang

Topics: Cannabis marketing, Social media advertising, Sexual scripts, Health communication

Sexual and romantic scripts are used to market cannabis products, now legal for adult-use in several U.S. states. We conducted an online experiment ( N = 747) examining the impact of viewing brand-generated social media posts promoting cannabis that included sexual, romantic, and non-sexual non-romantic recreational scripts among college students in Washington state. Increased perceptions that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex were associated with higher sex-related cannabis expectancies. Among men, wishful identification was associated with lower sexual risk expectancies among those who viewed sexual scripts and a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex among those who viewed sexual or romantic scripts. Among women, perceiving that ads suggested cannabis enhances sex was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex, whereas perceiving that ads suggested cannabis impacts sexual consent was associated with a lower likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Additionally, wishful identification among women was associated with a greater likelihood of intending to use cannabis before sex. Findings highlight associations between perceptions of brand-generated social media posts, expectancies, and intentions to use cannabis before sex among college students and identify mechanisms through which effects may occur.

item.title: Framing the regional frontlines: challenges, ethical dilemmas and experiences of Journalists in Northeast India
item.dc:creator: Sayan Dey
item.description:
Journalism · Sayan Dey

Topics: Journalistic role perceptions, Professional norms, Journalism studies, Digital journalism

This article investigates how journalists in Northeast India negotiate objectivity, ethics and journalistic role perceptions while covering conflicts in geo-politically sensitive and digitally mediated settings. Drawing on eight in-depth interviews, this study reveals how journalists navigate safety concerns, emotional connections and platform logics that increasingly affect their workflows. Employing Framing Theory and Role Theory, the paper highlights three interconnected dimensions: journalists’ reflexive negotiation between emotional attachment and professional neutrality, increasing influence of platform logics and analytics in editorial processes; and contextual restrictions arising from state control and linguistic hegemonies within the Indian national media landscape. The findings demonstrate that in conflict settings, journalistic objectivity is contextually negotiated rather than being universally fixed, highlighting moral sensitivities and hybrid professionalism in peripheral media settings. By examining the lived realities of journalists; the study contributes to de-Westernised discourses in Journalism Studies and explains how journalists in parts of the Global South, especially in conflict-sensitive and marginalised territories, reimagine journalistic ethics and agency amid political, cultural and technological challenges.

item.title: From “water, food, energy” to electoral legitimacy: media discourse and symbolic meaning-making in Romania’s 2024 election crisis
item.dc:creator: Antonio Amuza, Dan-Niculae PODARU
item.description:
Journalism · Antonio Amuza, Dan-Niculae PODARU

Topics: Populism, Political communication, Media framing, Discourse analysis

This article examines how populist political legitimacy is discursively constructed through semiotic framing in a context of democratic instability. Focusing on Romania’s 2024 presidential crisis, the study analyses how nationalist and anti-establishment meanings are produced, circulated, and recontextualized across digital and traditional media environments. Drawing on semiotic theory and critical discourse approaches, the article explores how recurring symbolic elements, such as sovereignty , moral purity , and elemental resources , operate as indexical signs that connect individual grievances to broader ideological narratives. The analysis combines qualitative discourse analysis of candidate communication, computational analysis of 10,556 news articles, and post-electoral survey data ( N = 572) collected immediately after the first round of voting. The analysis shows how discursive strategies contribute to processes of political legitimation by framing power relations in affective and moral terms rather than procedural or institutional ones. Empirical survey data are used to contextualize how these symbolic repertoires circulated across fragmented media environments and were associated with differentiated patterns of electoral alignment. The findings highlight the central role of media discourse and symbolic framing in shaping political legitimacy, polarization, and interpretive authority within contemporary hybrid media systems, offering insights into the symbolic mechanisms through which legitimacy is negotiated in post-socialist societies.

item.title: Authoritative Yet Conditionally Cohesive: The Cohesion Dynamics of Journalistic (Non-) Authority on Chinese TikTok (Douyin)
item.dc:creator: Peng Xiao, Wen Shi, Yangkun Huang
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Peng Xiao, Wen Shi, Yangkun Huang

Topics: Journalism, Short-form video, Platform affordances, Social media algorithms

The rise of algorithmic curation challenges the traditional authority of journalism. Focusing on Douyin, this study employed agent-based testing and temporal network analysis to examine how recommendation systems generate network cohesion around Chinese state and non-state media. Results revealed that state media’s cohesive power stemmed from news, whereas cohesion around non-state media was sustained by non-news content. However, for both media types, the cohesion generated by news showed a significant decline over time, and this trend varied by topic. These findings suggest that, beyond mere institutional status, strategic content adaptation is fundamental to building network cohesion in algorithmic environments.

item.title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
item.dc:creator: Dragoș M. Obreja
item.description:
New Media & Society · Dragoș M. Obreja

Topics: Algorithm awareness, Social media algorithms, TikTok, Social connectedness

This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

item.title: The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
item.dc:creator: Matilde Catanese
item.description:
New Media & Society · Matilde Catanese

Topics: Generative AI, Platform affordances, Misinformation, Digital media

This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

item.title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
item.dc:creator: Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton
item.description:
New Media & Society · Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton

Topics: Local news, Social currency, News consumption, Social influence
